Ix conjunction with Mr. HARRISON and my
brother, Mr. HENRY CROIkirTON, I last year
signed my name to the Report on the Trade
Union Act. Will you allow me to state very
briefly, and without indulging in personalties
hardly pertinent to the matter, my reasons for
adhering to the opinions expressed in the
following terms : "The whole of this statute
must be repealed."
Let me state, at the outset, that I think the
Bill which 1413 have several times heard is
"backed" (whatever the technical jargon may
mean) by certain able Liberal members, would
be, were it passed, decidedly an improvement
on the present law. This is especially the case
since the Bill, which I saw for the first time
last Monday, has been amended by the re-
moval of the clause to which Mr. IthutisoN
and Professor BEESLY so warmly objected.
Bat if any one will look at the Report to which
I have already referred, they will see that the
main part of it is as applicable to the new Bill
as to the old Act. Rave the following passages,
for instance, lost their applicability? The
new Act has been passed to prevent coercion
among workmen . . . it makes a number
of acts, many of which are perfectly harmless
and legitimate in themselves, crimes when
done by a workman in reference to his
employment, and with a view to coerce.
. • . The object of the Bill is to
put down coercion." Everything, therefore,
depends upon the meaning of the word coer-
cion, and yet there is no definition of coercion
in it, no limitation of it, so as to afford some
protection to workmen against its being inter-
preted in such a way which the Parliament
did not intend. Hence there is great danger
ofits being interpreted in such a way as to
include what may be called moral coercion,
that justifiable and proper influence which
each citizen is entitled to exercise over others.
Again, in allusion to the clause—retained in
this Bill—by which it is made an offence for

desire of making every little transgression on

Right and Duty are like two

that there are vast numbers of acts which
are morally wrong, and yet which cannot be
made criminal without causing grievous in-
justice. Such is this statute, and it has been
confided to the magistrates, country gen-

tlemen, and employers of labour who
have summary jurisdiction over all of-
fences committed under it." The present
Bill would, I admit, be an improvement
on the old Act, but it is not what we have
hitherto demanded; and the conduct of the
working class during the past year should not
teach them too much humility in this matter.
The strikes of the engineers at Newcastle, of
the labourers in Warwickshire, of the carters
at Liverpool, ought to have taught our
legislators that workmen are not all
Broadheads, and that a union may be used
for other purposes than putting needles
in brick clay. But there is one great
difference between the Act of last year and
the present Bill. Last year's statute was
roughhewn by a House of Commons, and
polished by a House of Lords. This is pro-
posed by our own side: "It was not mine
enemy (I quote from memory) that hath done
this thing; then I could have borne it. But
it was thou, mine own familiar friend." Nor ,
is the difference merely a technical one.
Assume we wore all agreed in supporting this
Bill, and got it' passed. Seeing ourselves so
successful, the following session we attempt
its total repeal. Shall we not be open to the
objection, "What, repeal this Bill? Was it
not prepared by your own friends, and
'backed' by , your own able supporters ?" It
is said, however, I believe, that the Bill is
not proposed because it is a good Bill, but
because it is likely to be passed. Now, lam not
of those who think a patient takes two halves of
a pill better than one whole one, and
I own, it appears to me just as unlikely that
the Lords should consent to a Bill, however
ably " backed," which calmly puts aside their
own pet amendment, as that they should
repeal the obnoxious measure altogether Of
course, they can be squeezed into doing either
the one or the other, but the amount of

requisite pressure would, roughly speaking, be
about the same in either case. The question
is more one of policy than of law, and of

course different views may be taken as to wha•
is the most prudent course to be adopted. :

have stated the reasons that led me to retain
our original opinion.
Some reference has been made to the views
of my brother, Mr. HENRY CaourroN, on this
matter. He will shortly be here to speak for
himself, but I may perhaps be allowed to say
that I talked with him on this subject shortly
before he left England, and nothing he then
said at all led me to understand that he has
deviated from the course he has always ad-
vocated—viz., an immediate and direct effort
to repeal the Bill in tot°.
ALBERT CROMPTON.

TM?, DELICATE QUESTION.

-
THE diseu9sioll in the BEE-InvE which has
grown out of the Contagions Diseases Acts,
affords some promise that "out of the strong"
may "come forth sweetness." Every right-
minded man ought to admire and rally round
those noble women who have taken up the
oause of their sex in this matter. In any
jemarks whioh I am about to offer, it will be

my rule to avoid the remotest personality.
Besides other objeotions lying against it, the
gist of the question is in danger of being
overlaid by a large quantity of irrelevant
surplusage.

For rai part, I am apt to suspect any merely
human legislation on behalf of which a moral
purpose is put forth. Acts of Parliament
may promote immorality ; but it is beyond the
powers of a statute to make either men or
women virtuous. Should the National Assembly
of France legislate for the revival of gaming-
houses, it would be a co-parent in the genera-
tion of vice wholesale; but, should it pass a
measure for the entire suppression of staking
money at play, it would only expose the
impotency of preceptive law.
For those medical and surgical men who
projected the statutes in question, and who
advocate their continuance and, extension, I
am able to make some apology. It is one of
the things incident to their noble profession,
as, indeed, to professions in general, that the
professors are apt either to exaggerate the
capabilities of their own line of things, or to
fix their eyes so exclusively upon it as to omit
considerations drawn from other sources, and
not less necessary to the formation of an
accurate judgment and a right handling of the
practical point.

The proper function of the medical and
surgical arts is the cure of internal disease
and external hurt. Wherever these are found,
there let the physician or the surgeon step in.
He is to heal the ailing if he can, and as soon
as he can, without the least reference to the
moral question, whether the patient has
or has not brought the ailment upon
himself by any fault of his own. I
do not say he is to stop here. He
may make society at large his debtors, by
warning the public against causes generative
of disease, or against the growth, spread, and
perpetuation of particular diseases, which,
beginning with undermining the strength of
individuals, proceed to poison the health of
whole families, and, transmitted from one
generation to another, finish by diffusing their
virulent ieaven through the whole com-
munity. For example, among the New
Zealanders, the North American Indians, and
other aboriginal tribes, personal commerce
with depraved and diseased Europeans has
been attended with consequences to themselves
which threaten their respective tribes with
total extinction.

In the war against such plagues as this,

the medical and surgical contingent is as
necessary, though fighting with different arms,
as are the forces composed of social reformers
and of religious teachers. Where the disciples
of GALEN and HIPPOCRATES miss their ways
is in meddling with matters of police.
We have ourselves to blame for encouraging
them to take a part in all the branches of
sanitary regulation and sanitary effort, in-
stead of restricting them to those branches
in which their special qualifications fit
them to advise and co-operate. It is not
a sounder maxim to keep the cobbler
to his last than it would be to keep the
physician ta his prescription and the surgeon
to his instrument-ease. Nobody ever found
fault with the institution of special hospitals
for the treatment of particular diseases. The
poor circumstances of many patients has made
this indispensable ; and the cost is paid in
the extended means of observation and cons-

parison thus afforded to scientific) men, who,
by such means, come to understand diseases
more thoroughly, and to treat them with
corresponding success.
But there is a wide difference between a
hospital into which all who need and will may
come, and a gaol, with the name of hospital,
into which men and women laid hold of by
the policeman may be forced, whether they
need or not, whether they will or not.
There is another distinction material to the
issue. Here are two infirmaries both erected
for the cure of one and the same complaint,
the sole difference between them is this, that,
whereas the first, supported by voluntary con-
tributions, simply admits applicants suffering
under the complaint, and retains them until
they are pronounced cured, the second,
established by law and sustained by the State,
is a place into which women, seized by the
police • on suspicion of the complaint, and
found, on compulsory examination, to be
subjects of it, are forced to go, and, remaining
until cured, are then sent out, with a certificate
of clean health, to resume that kind of life
in the pursuit of which they contracted the
ailment of which they have been oured.
The plea urged on behalf of the second of
these infirmaries is, the extirpation of the
complaint to the cure of which it is avowedly
devoted. It must be acknowledged, that such
women as may be cured in the first, are at
liberty to return to ways in which they will
be always liable to a recurrence of the com-
plaint. But the perfectly voluntary institution
has fulfilled its design; and if, during the period
of seclusion, any number of the patients are
not simply cured in body, but brought to a
sounder mind as to their future course, so
much the better for themselves and for
society. But how can it be pretended that
the first of these infirmaries extirpates, or
even tends to extirpate, the complaint? The
supposition of its very existence is that the
cured will go back to resume the very com-
merce with men or with women to which their
former infection was entirely due. So far as
their cure goes, it is for the purpose of pro-
moting that promiscuous intercourse between
the sexes which was the sourc.2, has been the
propagator, and will be the perpetuator of the
complaint, that, as is pretended, infirmary
number one exists to extirpate!
The cure of this complaint is one thing ; its
prevention, either as to individual oases or
with a view to extirpation, is another thing.
With the medical and surgical faculty we
must leave the former, not doubting
that, with impartial zeal, they will undertake
the deluded youth and the abandoned
woman, the patient who can fee them well and.
the sufferer who has nothing but thanks to
pay them with. But we shall only delude
ourselves if we fondly imagine that it is for
the whole Colleges of Physicians and Surgeons
put together, to prevent and extirpate this
fell and foul disease. The well is deep, and
they have nothing to draw with. The only
real security against it is to be found, as I

articles.text:
THE BALLOT BILL IN THE LORDS.

WE perceive all the Ministerial organs are
loud in their declamations against the Duke of
Icnuotro and the Peers, for having spoilt the
admirable Ballot Bill sent up to them by the
Commons. Now, we have no partioular venera-
tion for the House of Lords, and we have no
doubt that, in 011111101) with the aristocrats of
the Lower House in opposing the secret vote,
they were actuated by the desire of maintain-
ing the governing power in the hands of the
upper classes, and preventing the masses, or
working men, from having their due influence
in what is derisively called the People's
House.

Now, we propose in this article to prove that
the Ballot Bill amended in the House of
Commons, adopted by the Government, and sent
up by them to the Lords, was utterly worthless,
and that, although it has been tinkered at
by their lordships in their zeal against the
secret vote, it has not .been rendered in. the
slightest degree worse than it wr..s when it
left the hands of Mr. ULADSTONE and Mr.
FORSTER. The Government journals say, that
by the Duke of RIMIALOND'S amendment of
the second clause, the secret vote is made
optional. No doubt of it; but not more so
than it was in Mr. GLADSTONE'S Bill. The
Amendment o fthe Lords expressly enacts that
the elector, if he pleases, mayemark pubiiely on
the ballot paper the candidate for whom he
votes. Now what does Mr. GLiDSTONE'S Bill
do? It requires the voter to go into a secret
compartment to mark his ballot paper. So
far, so good. But then this same Ministerial
Bill allows the voter to op3n his Ballot paper
when he returns to the public eomparttneut,
and display to the agents and all the othat
persons in the room how his Ballot paper is

marked. I beg leave to ask, then, if there
is anything more than a mere verbal
difference betwixt the Duke of RICIDIOND'S
Bill and Mr. GLIDSIONE'S Bill. There is as
much right of option in the elector to. vote
secretly iu the one case as in the other.

I perceive that several of the Ministerial
papers are attempting to draw a distinction.
They say that, although by the Government
Bill the elector can display his marked Ballot
paper to the public, he makes himself liable to
be charged with a misdemeanour in doing so.
Now, there is not one word in the Ministerial
Bill which enacts anything of the kind. On
the bontrary, by a vote of the House of Com-
mons, it is declared perfectly legal for the
elector to display his Ballot paper. On the
18th of April last the Government moved the
following clause :—" No voter shall, after
marking his vote on his Ballot paper, display
such paper in such a manner as to make
known to any person the name of the candi-
date for or against whom he has so marked
his vote." This proposed Ministerial clause
was rejected by a majority of the lime of
Commons, and the optional right of the
elector to vote secretly or not fully established.
Notwithstanding which, the Bill was fully
accepted by Mr. GLADSTONE and sent up to
the Lords. The difference betwixt Mr. GLAD.
STONE and the Duke of RICHMOND is merely'
a question of Tweedledum and Tweedledee.
We are surprised that the Duke of RICHMOND
did not accept Mr. GLADSTONE'S Bill without
any alteration whatever. It would as
effectually have served the purpose of the
Tories as his own. The fact is, neither the
Tories nor the Ministerial Liberals desire a
real Ballot Bill. The Ballot Bill was in-
troduced by Mr. GLADSTONE as a mere rally-
ing cry for party purposes. Had he been
sincerely and honestly in favour of the secret
vote, he would have acted like Earl GREY
in 1330. He would have introduced a full
and complete measure upon which he
would have taken his stand; and. he
should have informed his party that he
would allow iv) amendments in which prin-
ciple- was involved, and that if any such
were carried, he would throw up the Bill and
dissolve Parliament, or resign. Had Mr.
GLADSTONE acted in this way, all the real
Liberals would have joined him. The con-
stituencies, nearly to a man, would have been
with him, and he would have ca,rried the
Ballot as triumphantly, and much more easily
through both Houses, than did. Earl Gas!
the Reform Bill of 1832. But alas Mr.
Inaigrrozan is neither an Earl GREY flora
Lord PALMERSTON, with his strong tact and
common sense. He is nothing more than a

THE CRIIIINAL, LAW AMENDMENT

The member for Lincoln has long been familiar

amendment will have the effect of confining

last is a valuable proviso. The Bill thus

and they can support it without putting them-
selves in a false position by re-enacting the

We thought right. And our recommending

articles.title: MR. DISRAELI ON RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.
articles.text:
MR. DISRAELI ON RELIGIOUS EDUCA-
TION.

Mn. DISRAELI'S speech on National Educa-
tion delivered at a recent meeting of the
"National Society for Promoting the Educa-
tion
•of the Poor in the Principles of the
Established Church," should not be overlooked.
The Archbishop of CANTERBURY was in the
chair, surrounded by Bishops, Lords, Illustrious
Commoners, Reverends, and others who feel,
or profess to feel, a strong interest in the
:welfare of the poor, and who aim at obtaining
for them multiplied spiritual graces, but who,
somehow or other, utterly fail, oven in the
most trivial attempts to improve the worldly
condition of poor men.
Amidst this assemblage of illustrious per-
sonages, Mr. Drsitiru was the central figure.
It was to him the Archbishop, the Bishops, the
Lords, the Commoners, the Reverends, and all
others listened for those utterances, by which
to plan how to make the best of both worlds for
"the poor" was to be made known. The task,
so far as words went, has seldom been so well
performed. The hon, gentleman's language
was all that could be desired—sonorous and
well-measured, sparkling but not meretri-

_
eious, rising occasionally into the region of
fancy, but never leaving the solid ground of
fact and argument. His speech was, in fact,
as SIDNEY Sum would say, all this, and a
great many other things without a great many
• other things.
"The' deep, yet clear; the' gentle, yet not dull;
Strong without rage; without o'er-flowing full."
The honourable gentleman said all that
could be said for his clients, but occasionally
his eagerness its an advocate carried him too
far. Sometimes his arguments came back
like the boomerang, and hit himself. It is not
easy to keep within the bounds of common-
sense when urging a sect forward in a work
of proselytism; and when common-sense has
been abandoned, self-contradiction is not
difficult. In the very nature of things, an
expectant Prime 'Minister must be severe on
the actual possessor of office. It was proper
enough, therefore, that Mr. DISRAELI should
be very severe on Mr. GLADSTONE for Elba-
eating his duty in giving up religious teaching
by the State. But, supposing this charge
true—which it is not—why does its utterer
soon after inform his bearers that their " meet-
ing of that day will have been the commence-
ment of a movement which will give a new
colour and life. to the great question of
National Education," If Mr. DISRAELI and
his Episoopal friends are about to give a new

"colour and life" to ri ational Education, then
GLa.nstortz, arousing them to action, has
certainly done more good than harm, and
whoever else may complain, the friends of the
Church ought to be satisfied.
But Mr. DISRAELI deplores the determination
of the State not to "supply or regulate the
religious instruction 'of the people." If Mr.
DISRAELI was in power, this supplying and
regulating religious instruction would no doubt
be regarded as a parasnount duty; but he ought
to tell us how he would perform this duty in
detail. Of course, he could not have Church
of England teaching alone. the past history of
the world has proved the impolicy of this, and
holds in overflowing record its mischievous-
ness and the misery it has caused. Mr.
DISRAELI would no doubt give freedom of
teaching to all religious bodies, and State aid
even to the most unorthodox. He'd lump them,
for liberty's sake, and tolerate them because it
was convenient to do so, whilst at most he
could scarcely be expected to believe in more
than one of them himself. He knows very
well, for he has sprung from one of the most per-
secuted bodies of believers, that persecution has
usually been indulged in by State-taught and
State-supported creeds, and that it was chiefly
when religious bigots could call to their aid. the
power of intriguing politicians, that earth
became cursed by those worst of all atrocities
called religious persecutions. Let the history
of the Jews testify to this, from the massacres
of the middle ages to the present Roumanian
blood-letting, not forgetting the Holy-cross
day at Rome, when this poor persecuted people,
until recently, were driven to mass—
"Spurred through the Corso, stripped to the
waist;
Jew-brutes, with sweat and blood well spent
To usher in worthily Christian Lout."
But then, unless the State supplies and re-
gulates religious instruction, if Mr. DISIIA.ELI
speak the truth, we shall fail to recognise
"the providential government of the world and
the future responsibility of man." Let this
utterer of high-sounding sophism look to the
history of the people to whom he belongs by
, blood. What State, what Government has
attended to the religious instruction of the
Jews ? What Christian government in
Europe, at any time, or in any way,
undertook the responsibility of instructing
the children of the Jews, in Bible,
Mishua, or Gemara ? What Arch
bishop of CANTERBURY or other dignitary of
our Established Church charged himself with
keeping alive in the minds of Jews "the
providential government of the world and the
future responsibility of man," except to re-
mind them of GOD'S wrath rather than His
justice? And yet, if Mr. DISRAELI will try
to remember facts, he will find the most
abundant proof that this faithful, but much
persecuted. people never lost their belief in
" the providential government of the world,
and the future responsibility of man."
Let Mr. DISRAELI and his clerical adnifrors
increase their schools as rapidly as they can, and
proselytise wherever they have a chance. Let
them push religiouS teaching as a State poll.'
amongst "the poor," that the people by such
means may be made more obedient to their
pastors and masters. That which is a policy
and a hypocrisy with politicians in search of
preferment, may become sincere piety in
others. Like begets like in appearance as
well as in reality.
Hypocrisy may do as well
To propagate a Church as zeal;
So round white stones will serve, they say,
As well as eggs, to make hem lay.

On this matter, the words of Mr. DISRA.ELI
cannot be mistaken. Out of the fulness of the
heart the mouth will speak. He betrays him-
self without being aware of it. In his zeal as
'recruiting-sergeant for the Church the truth
comes out. Here are his words—" To obtain
a great hold upon the education of the nation is
to possess ourselves of the mind of the people.''
What can be plainer than this, or what more
significant when applied to the children of the
poor? It is the'old practice frankly insisted
on as a future policy. It is equivalent to say-
ing, "Lay hold of poor men's children, and
shape them into tools for the use of others.
Teach them brute obedience as a religious
duty due
.to gart, but to be paid to those
placed over thera by the ivine Will." This is
what is called educating them for their posi-

tion, and unhappily making true the poet's
words in regard to the poor :
So that ye for than are made
Loom and plough, and sword and spade;
With or without your own will; bent
To their defence and nourishment.
Religion, as a true and a holy thing, may do
for the uninitiated, the simple-minded babes
and sucklings. But by great statesmen—future
Premiers—it is to bi regarded as a wholesome
restraint, an instrument of authority like the
parish stooks or the prig' pound, to hold.
stray sinners by the heels. Exalted people
profit by it; humble-minded, lowly men
should be taught when young to believe
Dr. jOILNSON said Something Might be made
of a Sootehman if he was caught young. Mr.
DISRAELI believe that the Church and State
May get possession of the public mind in the
same way by catching the children in time.
To be fore-warded is to be fore-armed. Let
working men take the hint, and if the Church
and the coming PRIME MINISTER will spread
their nets for poor men's children, let them be
compelled to do so at. their own expense.
When such mere political and sectarian
schemers are thrust aside, loftier ideas of
religion may find an easier and more willing
acceptance by the people. At present• the
example in high places is a bad one. Con-
spicuously before the eyes of all is to be seen
a theology without religion—a husk of creed
without a kernel of faith; and side by side
with this, in polities, a substitution of faction
for patriotism. Never was it more needed than
now, that an awakening people—sincere in their
faith whatever that faith may be, honest in
their political oonvictions and patriotic ispira-
tions—should breathe the breath of life and
healing into our fashionable putrefaotions
—religious and political.

articles.title: STRIKE AND LOCK-OUT OF THE LONDON BUILDING TRADES.
articles.text:
STRIKE AND LOCK-OUT OF
THE LONDON BUILDING
TRADES.

The determined and now openly hostile con-
test between operatives and employers in the
building trade has actually commenced, and it
will be useful to review the successive stages
of the agitation and contest. The claim of the
men was for a working day of nine hours and
pay at the rate of ninepence. an hour. These
terms the masters refused to give, and a strike
was decreed at two firms. Those of Mr. Brass
and Messrs. Jackson and Shaw were selected,
and the men in their employ were called out,
with the understanding that they would be
supported in the strike out of the earnings of
their comrades until the firms in question had
succumbed, and the masters had given the
terms throughout the trade. With this mode
of fighting the masters were not content, and
accordingly they met and placed before the
men proposals for terminating the dispute by
arbitration, and they made it an essential con-
dition that pending arbitration the strike
already declared should cease. In default of
agreement, and in the event of the strike
being maintained, they notified their inten-
tion of resorting to a lock-out on a given day.
The men accepted the principle of arbitra-

tion, and sent a deputation to confer with the
masters on the form and scope which the
arbitration should receive. But it soon
appeared very doubtful whether the men wore
really prepared, as regarded the essential
matter of dispute, for any arbitration at all,
and at length it was determined to collect the
votes of the men by formal inquiry, pending
which the masters agreed to postpone the
lock-out, which had been fixed for Monday

last. On Tuesday the results of the voting of
the men were declared, and with a conclusion
perfectly decisive. They absolutely refused to
let the question of working time and wages go
out of their hands, and pronounced almost
unanimously against withdrawing the strike
already commenced. The masters, therefore,
have locked out, so that the men on strike
against the selected firma will no longer be
supported from the earnings of their brethren,
and the fight will be general. The following
report is a consecutive history of the dispute
since our last week's issue.

init.

Mr. Greedy replied that the delegates, while in
favour of arbitration as a principle, were not dis-
posed to consent to 'arbitrate under the throat of
a lock-out.

The Chairman saidthe men had invited a lock-out
by the strike. lie wished to know what powers
the deputation possessed.
Mr. hlatkin, the secretary, here banded to the
chairman the resolution passed by a large majority
at the meeting of the delegates on Thursday
night, which was as 1)110w8 :—" That the deputa-
tion be instructed strictly to adhere to:the terms of
the memorial already presented to the master
builderm—yiz., nine hours at 9d. the hour, but

with full power to arbitrate on the code of working
rules, and the men on strike to remain out until
the question is settled.
The Chairman said it was much to be regretted
that the deputation had not been invested with
full powers to treat. Time was pressing. In the
face of the resolutions just read he could see no
alternative for the employers but to carry into
effect the lock-out on Monday n ext, the notices
for which had been already posted at most of the
building firms.
After considerable discussion, the Chairman
then read over :the propositions which had been
heard by the Committee of masters, and which
appeared in our last week's issue. The question
now simply was, were the deputation attending
on behalf of the men prepared to accept these
propositions. If so, thoy could at once proceed to
consider the appointment of the arbitrators or
referees. His idea was that the whole question
should be discussed by four employers and
four workmen in the presence of the arbitrators ,
who should then give their decision after ha.reing
both sides. He suggested that the deputation
from the delegates should retire into another room,
and consider what course they were prepared to
adopt.

This suggestion was complied with, the deputa-
tion having been first supplied with a copy of the
propositions or resolutions. After an absence of
about a quarter of an hour, on their return,
Mr. Sinclair said the deputation could not,
consistently with the instructions they had
received, accept either the first or third proposi-
tions, but they could accept the second relating to
the working rules. Tho deputation would, how-
ever, lay the whole of the propositions before the
delegates at their meeting on Saturday, and take

their: opinion upon them.
Messrs. Smith, Sadler, end Greedy, the other
members of the deputation, spoke to the same
effect.

The Chairman said this would be too late to
prevent the look-out, all the arrangements having
been made. It would, in reality, commence on
Saturday.
Another long discussion hero ensued, both
parties evincing a desire to avoid a lock-out if
possible, the deputation requesting that proper
time might be afforded for the delegates to consider
the proposals by the lock-out being suspended, and
the masters replying that the deputation had it in
their power to prevent the lock-out by assenting
to the proposal that the men on strike should
resume work. For ROM time neither party would
give way, and the conference was on the point
of breaking off without any result, when
Mr. Lucas suggested that if the deputation
could not themselves accept the proposals, they
might agree to recommend them for the adoption
of the delegate meeting. If they would agree to
that course the masters would consent to suspend
the lock-out until Wednesday, which would give the
delegates bufficiont time to consider the proposals.
This led to another discussion and the drawing up
of the following document, which was ultimately
signed by the members of the deputation :
"That this deputation, representing the car-
penters and joiners of London, request the Com-
mittee of the Master Builders' Association to
suspend the operation of their resolution to lock-
out on Monday next until Wednesday, the 19th;
and, on consideration of their acceding to this
request, wo undertake to recommend to the accept-
ance of tho delegates the resolutions or proposals
presented to us this day as a fair and reasonable
mode in which a settlement of the matters in
dispute may be arrived at."
It was then arranged that the Secretary of the
Nine Hours' Committee should scud in to the
Secretary of the Masters' Committee, not later
than Tuesday morning, the result of the delegates'
voting upon the reiolutions to be submitted to
them by the deputation, and that circulars be at
once sent elf by the Committee to the various
firms, requesting them to suspend the lock-out
until Wednesday.

MEETING Or TILE DELEGATES AND REPORT or

DEPUTATION.

On Saturday evening the delegates from the
various societies and firms connected with the
building trade took place at the Brown Bear,
Bloomsbury, for the purpose of receiving a report
as to the interview between a deputation appointed
on behalf of the employes with the committee
of the masters. Mr. Sadler presided.
The Chairman said, when the deputation waited
upon the masters' committee on Friday they found
that the committee had a reporter present, and
they also asked pertnission to have a reporter
present, which was at once acceded to, The re-
port of the proceedings which took place between
the delegates' deputation and the masters' com-
mittee WM then read. The chairman said the
deputation unhesitatingly refused to refer either
the question of the nine hours or the 9d. to arbi-
tration, but expressed their willingness to do

so with reference to establishing a code
of rules. Upon being informed that the men
were determined to insist on their program°, that
from the Ist of July the work should be 51 hours
per week, and 9d. per hour, Mr. Hannon (the
masters' chairman) said it was no use proceeding
further, and the deputation were about to with-
draw, when it was suggested that they should
retire and consider the masters' resolutions, in
order to avert a lock-out on Monday, which would
not be withdrawn unless the men on strike returned
to their work pending an arbitration. The ultimate
result was that an agreement was come to that
upon the deputation aonsenting to lay before the
men and delegates and recommend the adoption of
the masters' resolutions that night the lock-out
should be postponed till Wednesday morning
awaiting their decision. In compliance with that
pl e he, as Chairman, now laid the masters'
resolutions before the delegates ; but, although
they were pledged to recommend them, the dele-
gates were in no way pledged. The course they
proposed to adopt was not to call upon the delegates
to come to a vote that night, but to convey the
resolutions to their respective shops, and meet
there again to decide the question.
The report having been received, a long discus-
sion ensued upon the masters' resolutions to
submit the 9d. per hour and nine hours per day to
arbitration, and to agree to a code of rules, upon
condition that those out on strike shall return to
their work. Very strong objections were raised
to having to settle the question by Monday night,
on account of want of time.

--- -
Mr. Binney moved a resolution to the effect
that every delegate here assembled should call his
constituents together on Monday next, to submit
the resolution adopted at the masters' meeting, and
that the delegates meet at nine o'clock on Tuesday
morning to report the result to the masters.
A Delegate from Poplar seconded this resolu-

The Chairman said he was in possession of the
copies of documents which the masters had
issued, threatening the lock-out on Wednesday
morning, and therefore they must give the masters
an answer not later than Tuesday morning.
An amendment was moved expressing regret at
the unsatisfactory result of the interview with the
masters, and determining to adhere to the claims of
the mon who are out on strike, but it was ulti-
mately withdrawn, and on a show of hands the
resolution was declared carried by 101 against 6.

articles.title: DECISION OF TUE WORKMEN.
articles.text:
DECISION OF TUE WORKMEN.

On Tuesday morning, at nine o'clock, the
delegates of the carpenters and joiners, to the
number of over 225, re-assembled at the Brown
Bear, Bloomsbury, for the purpose of reporting the
result of the voting of the men they represented
upon the proposal submitted to them by the com-
mittee of masters as their ultimatum prior to a

lock-out. Mr. Sadler occupied the chair.
The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said
the committee, with the view of enabling the meti

to vote distinctly upon the masters' prop-osals, had
divided thorn into three, so that the men might
unmistakeably express their opinions upon each of
three point. He hoped it would also be clearly
undert.tood that the votes only of those men would
be recorded who paid their weekly levy of is. to
the movement, and that the constituents of any
&legate who had not met together since Saturday
last could not be allowed to vote. This regula-

tion would, of course, materially reduce the
number of men voting, but the committee con-
sidered it only fair both to the masters and to the
movement that their resolutions should be strictly
enforced. (Cheers.) The proposals of the masters
had been divided into three points, and a separate
vote would be received on each of the three points.
It must be clearly understood that if the first
proposal, for the men on strike at once resuming
work, was rejected, the masters, or a
certain portion of them, were pledged to a lock-
out. He hoped the proceedings would be con-
ducted in an orderly and becoming manner, be-
fitting the gravity of the occasion. He then read
the three proposals to be voted upon as follows :
" 1. For and against the men now on strike
from the firms of Mr. Brass and Messrs. Jaokson
and Shaw resuming work at once upon the old
terms, pending any arbitration that may take
place. 2. For and against submitting the question of
the nine hours and 9d. per hour to arbitration. 3.
For and against holding a conference of an equal
number of masters and workmen to consider if any
code of working rules can be arranged for the
better regulation of the trade."
The Secretary then called upon each delegate in
rot ition to give in his return of the number of
paying members be represented, and the number
voting for and againtt each proposal. The
total number of men voting was about 4,000,
but as the results only were supplied to the
reporters the exact numbers voting for and against
each proposal cannot be given; but it was ascer-
tained that only about 350 voted for the first Po*

P 024 for the men on strike resuming work; that
the votes in favour of the second proposal for sub-
mitting the nine hours and the 9d. to arbitration
was under 1,250; while the voting for the third
Proposal, of holding a conference of masters and
Workmen on a code of working rules, was almost
Unanimous in its favour.

'Upon the reporters being re-admitted to the
room, they having been requested to retire while
the secretaries were casting up the numbers,

The Chairman said he declared the first pro-
posal to be rejected by an overwhelming majority;
the second proposal for arbitration had been
rejected by a large majority; while the third
proposal had been nearly unanimously adopted.
This announcement was received by the dele-
gates with loud cheering, followed by "Three
cheers for the nine hours and Od. per hour."

A resolution was then moved- that the result
of the voting he taken to the Masters' Committee
by a deputation of four delegates, but this was
7ery strongly opposed by the great majority, and
it was ultimately resolved that the secretary should
enclose the result to the committee of masters in
a letter sent by a special messenger, which was
accordingly done, and the meeting adjourned.

articles.title: MASTERS ORDER A LOCE•OUT.
articles.text:
THE MASTERS ORDER A LOCE•OUT.

The Masters' Committee met at the Freemasons'
Tavern, at four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon to
consider the answer of the men to their proposals,
as shown by the voting. Mr. Hannen occupied
the chair, and amongst those present were Mepsrs.
C. Lucas, H. G. Smith, W. Brass, B. Stanley, G..
P. Trollope, G. Dines, F. Dove, G. Bird, G.
Jackson, Scrivener, Manly, G. Myers, &c.
After the meeting the following was sent down
to the representatives of the press in attend-
ance :-

(Copy of a letftr to be addressed to all the master

builders.)
11Freemasons' Tavern, J.une 18.
".Bnt,—The carpenters, joiners, and masons
luavlng refused to refer the question now in dispute
between themselves and the master builders to
arbitration, or to withdraw the strike at the works
of Mr. Brass and Messrs. Jackson and Shaw, you
are earnestly requested to carry out the resolution
passed at a meeting of the metropolitan master
'builders on the 7th of June by closing all shops
and works telonging to you within the district
over which the district surveyors have jurisdiction
until such time as Messrs. Jackson and Shaw and
Mr. Brass shall inform the committee of the
Master Builders' Association that they have been
able to resume their work.—Yours faithfully,

(Signed) "STANLEY G. BIRD, Hon. See. pro tem.',

CONTINUTION OF MASTERS LOCKOUT.

The men in all the firms went to work at six
o'clock on Wednesday morning as usual, and
worked on up to dinner time, twelve o'clock, with-
out receiving any notice. On their return, however,
from dinner, in the firms mentioned below, the
men were informed that the shops would be
closed at five o'clock until further notice, and that
they must remove their tools, and also that they
would be paid the money due to them by apply-
ing at the cashier's office. The men were fully
prepared for this notice, and no surprise or excite.
ment was caused.

The following firms have closed their establish-
ments :—Messrs.' Holland and Hannon, Blooms-
bury; Myers and Son, Lambeth; Coils and Sons
Camberwell; Henshaw and Co., City-road;
Adamstm and Son, Turnham-green ; Ashby and
Homer, Whitechapel ; Cubitt and Co., Gray's-inn-
road; Baker and Co., Stangate ; Gammon and
Co., Lambeth; Manley and Rogers, Camden-
town; Simpson and Co., Tottenham-court-road;
Patrick and Sons, Westminster-road; Smith and
Taylor, Pimlico; Freake and Co., Chelsea;
Messrs. Lucas and Co., Lambeth; Trollope and
Sons, ; Dines and Banderet, Pimlico;
Hill and Sons, Islington; Dove and Co., Isling-
ton; Scrivener and White, Camden-town, and
others. In the aggregate these firms employ
about 10,000 men in the various branches of
the building trade, the whole of whom are thus
thrown out of employment.

articles.title: PAYMENT OF TUE MEN ON STRIKE.
articles.text:
PAYMENT OF TUE MEN ON STRIKE.

The receipts of the Carpenters' Nino Hours
Committee during the last week, including the
balance of £73 in hand, amounted to nearly
£5OO. On Wednesday morning the men on strike
were paid their second week's strike pay of 275.
per man, absorbing nearly £4OO.

articles.title: STONE MASONS.
articles.text:
THE STONE MASONS.

On Monday night a crowded meeting of the
London operative masons, who have memorialized
the master builders for the same terms as the
carpenters and joiners-51 hours per week, at 9d.
per hour—was held at Wileocke's Assembly.
rooms, Westminster-road, Mr. Ketteringham in
the chair, for the purpose of receiving a report
from a deputation of the Masons' Committee, who
on Monday afternoon met the Masters Builders'
Committee at the Freemasons' Tavern.

L. Mr, Weighill, the- ficCret4try, otatcd that lasi

week the Masons' Committee, upon hearing that
the Masters' Committee had appointed to meet a
deputation from the carpenters, instructed him to
write to the masters' secretary, to the effect that as
the masons were moving for the same object as the
carpenters, they considered a deputation from their
body should also be present, or otherwise they
should not feel bound by any decision that might
be arrived at. To this request they received no
reply previous to the carpenters' deputation being
received, but on Saturday afternoon a notice was
sent to them by Mr. Bird, the masters' secretary,
that they would be prepared to meet a deputation
from the masons on Monday. The deputation had
accordingly waited upon the masters that day.
Mr. Broadhurst, a member of the deputation,
then reported the details connected with the
interview. Himself and his colleagues, Messrs.
Nesbitt, Kinnaird, Bowman, and the secretary
proceeded at two o'clock that afternoon to the
Freemasons' Tavern, where they met the same
gentlemen who had received the deputation from
the carpenters, Messrs.
,Hannen, Lucas, Trollope,
Dines, and the secretary, Mr. Bird. After some
general remarks, the deputation were asked
whether they were prepared to submit the question
of the nine hours and 9d. per hour to arbitration.
The deputation objected to enter into any discus-
sion upon the question of arbitration unless the
threat of a lock-out, at least so far as the masons
were concerned, was withdrawn. The chairman
said this distinction could not be made. The de-
putation reminded the committee that the
memorial of the men had been before the masters
for some months without any reply being given,
andnow they were to be forced into a hurriedarbi-
tration under threat of a lock-out. The only reply
made by the chairman was the handing to the
deputation of the resolution signed on Friday by
the carpenters' deputation. Mr. Lucas said he
supposed the masons had the same notice of the
look-out as the carpenters. The deputation
informed the masters that they considered a con-
ference such as they wore then holding was quite
as capable of discussing and settling the question
as any strangers who might be called in, un-
acquainted with the trade, They considered it
was futile to attempt to patoh up the question.
The men were resolved upon having the nine
hours, and the question would come up again
next year. These annual agitations were injurious
alike to both masters and men. Afker a long dis-
cussion tho deputation laid the following proposal
before the masters committee, which, if accepted
by them, they would lay before the men for
approval, but, if the committee refused, it was not
to be afterwards used by the masters to the
prejudido of the memorial. This proposal was
that 63 hours should constitute a week's work, at
bid. per hour until the Ist of March, 1873, after
which date the wages should be 9d. per hour.
After some hesitation this proposal was rejected
by the Masters' Committee, who again said the
original terms of the memorial, 51 hours at 9d. per
hour, must be submitted to arbitration. The
deputation said they had no power to agree to
arbitration; all that they could promise was to
take the opinion of the men upon the question
that evening. The conference then ended, haVing
lasted more than two hours.

The above report having been received, a long
discitssion ensued, and it could not be clearly ascer-
tained, as there was no strike at present among the
masons, whether, if they consented to arbitration,
the lock-out would be enforeed against them, sup-
posing the carpenters on at' Ike refused to resume
work pending the arbitration, in accordance with
the masters' resolution. Ultimately,
Mr. Salter moved the following resolution :

That we, the masons of London, do not admit
of arbitration on the questien of the nine hours
and the 9d. per hour, but that we adhere tri ally
to the terms of our memorial—namely, 51 hums
per week at 91 per hour.
' - -

He said they had been agitating the nine-hour
question for the last 15 years, and they bad never
before been in so good a position to obtain it.
They must not throw away the opportunity.
Mr. Skrernp seconded the resolution.
Mr. Nesbitt moved as an amendment,
That the whole question be left in the hands of
the committee."

He reminded the meeting that the adoption of
the resolution would bring about a look-out.

Mr. Stockton seconded the amendment.

Mr. Parker moved as a rider :

"That we accept 51 hours per week at 81d. per
hour until the Ist of March, 1873, when there
shall be a rise to 9cl. per hour.

Mr. Worsun2 seconded the rider.

Another disoussion ensued, after which the vote
was taken, when both rider and amendment were
lost, but few hands being held up for either. The
original resolution refusing arbitration was then
carried by a very large majority, followed by loud
cheering.
The proceedings theu terminsted.

articles.title: FAIDAY MORNING.
articles.text:
FAIDAY MORNING.

The carpenters and joiners met last evening at
the Brown Bear, Bloomsbury. Mr. Sadler in the
chair. The delegates brought in reports of the
look-out, and it was found that about thirty of the
largest firms had closed their shops. A mass of
detailed business was then transacted, such as
appointing district committees, electing delegates
to visit the large provincial towns to solicit assis-
tance for the men locked out, and other] arrange-
ments for carrying on the struggle.
The following appeal has been issued :

THE LOCH-OUT OF CARPENTERS AND JOINERS OF

LONDON.

FELLOW WontatEN,—We, the operative car-
penters and joiners of London, have been agitating
to obtain a reduction in the working hours from
66i to 61 per week, and an advance from Bd. to
Od per hour, making a difference of 7d. per week
in our present rate of wages, and to further that
object have been compelled to take decided action
by withdrawing a considerable number of men
from their employ. In consequence of that action
the employets have locked out the whole of the
trade, because the men that were withdrawn have
not resumed work on the old terms. Under these
circumstances, we earnestly solicit your assistance
in the struggle which, if gained, must prove
beneficial to the trade at large.
The committee sit daily at the Brown Bear,
Broad-street, Bloomsbury, from 9 a.m. till 8 pan.,
to receive subscriptions.
Taos. ITALL, Treasurer.
CHAS. Kellam, Secretary.

P.O. Orders to be sent to the Secretary, made
payable to Thomas Ilall, Treasurer, at the Post-
office, Broad-street, Bloomsbury.

The masons met last night at Wilcock's looms,
Lambeth, Mr. Ketteringham in tho chair.
It was a special meeting of the trade, under the
following circumstances :—lt appeared from what
was stated at the meeting that under the Lock-Out
resolutions of the masters they had made a special
exception in the cases of Mr. Brass and Messrs..
Jackson and Shaw, who were to be allowed to keep
their works open to the masons, bricklayers,
painters, and plasterers, and that a notice had been
posted by Mr. Brass at his job at the new Post.
office, where a large number of masons are em-
ployed, that the works would not be suspended.
The meeting, was, therefore, to consider the pro-
priety of calling mit the whole of the masons
working for these twe firms. After some discus-
sion it was resolved to call out the men and fight
the masters on their own plan.

articles.title: PROVINCIAL BUILDING TRADES.
articles.text:
THE PROVINCIAL BUILDING
TRADES.

LEEDS BRICKLAYERS' STRIKE.

At a meeting of the master bricklayers of Leeds,
held on Saturday evening at the Wheat Sheaf,
Upperhead-row, it was unanimously resolved—
" This meeting having again carefully considered
the position of matters as between the masters and
the operative bricklayers and labourers, also the
concessions made, namely, of an advance of wages
to 74d. per hour for bricklayers and 5111. per hour
for labourers, apprentices to be legally bound for
not less than five years, walking time allowed to
men sent to work out of town, and time and a half
for all overtime after the first two hours, cannot
make any further change in its decision."

THE 'BRADFORD JOINERS AND CARPENTERS.

On Saturday evening a meeting of the men
engaged in these trades at Bradford and distliet,
was held in the Secular Hall, Southgate. lir. C.
Aspinall was called to the chair, and he explained
that the object of the meeting was to ask for a
reduction of the hours of labour, and a rise in the
amount of wages paid. Society and non-society
men were present. A resolution was moved and
seconded that twelve months' notice be given to
the employers for a reduction of one hour per
week, the men to leave at twelve o'clock on
Saturday instead of one o'clock, as at present, and
that the rate of wages paid be 61d. per hour, an
advance of one halfpenny, which it was contended
by the proposer would be equal to an advance of
2s. Id. per week, the rate per hour now being
sixpence. It was moved, as an amendment, that
the rate be 'ad. per hour, or £1 9s. 11d, per week
for 49/ hours work, that it be the standard rate of
wages, to come into operation on the first Satur -
day or pay day in June, 1873, and that in the
event of any alteration afterwards six months'
notice to be given by either side. The rule
to be equally binding on the employers and the
workmen. After some discussion, in which
opinions varied as to the desirabili.y of establish-
ing a standard rate of wages, the amendment was
carried by a large majority, and a committee was
chosen to draw up a circular for transmission to
the employers, and to raise the necessary funds to
defray expenses.

THE COAL MINERS.

TUB EIGIIT lIOURS AGITATION IN STAFFOILDBIIIIiE.

On Friday night a meeting of South Stafford-
shire miners, representing the Wolverhampton,
Wednesbury, Willenhall, Bilston, Brownhills,
Walsall, and surrounding districts, was held at.
the Queen's Head Inn, Darlaston. Mr. William
Fulford took the chair.

Mr. Carter considered that as the ironworkers
were about to confer on the question of increased
wages, and as the miners generally regarded any
action by the ironworkers for an advance of wag, s
as a criterion for their taking similar steps, they
(the miners) had recently determined to agitate
for an advance of wages, and for a reduction in
the working time of one hour per day.
Mr. Gething (miners' agent for the district)
said the miners wanted only a fifth of the large
profits that were now being so generally received.
Tho men had taught the employers this lesson—
that they were perfectly able, in spite of contrary
protestation, to give the concession. It was time
for them to receive another lesson, and, if they
were peaceable and earnest in what they asked
for, they would give it. (Hear, hear.) He
earnestly called upon the men to be calm in their
behaviour, but firm in the course they took.
Mr. Cotterell moved the following resolution.:—
" That this meeting, considering the advance in
the price of iron and coal, is of opinion that.the
miners of the district are entitled to an advance
of 10 per cent., and a reduction of one hour per
day in their hours of labour."
The motion was seconded by Mr. Carter and
carried.

A vote of thanks
.to the chairman closed the
meeting.

TUUIATkNED STRIKII IN SOUTH

Throughout the coal district
.between Sholliohi
and Barnsley the greatest agitation .prevails with
regard to the question of wages. The South
Yorkshire Miners' Association delegates agreed at
a recent meeting to ask for an advance of wages to
the extent of 16 per cent. The men, however,
have found fault with the delegates, and appear to
have taken the mutter into their own hands.
They state that in the Leeds district 20 per cent.
has been conceded, and that they themselves should
have at least the same amount. On Saturday
morning the men at the New Oaks Colliery, Barns-.
lay, struck in a body. In the afternoon'a, meeting
was held. One of the speakers said that the
colliers found that as they got the best coal for
Is. 3d. per ton and the clay seam for Is, Id., the
10 per cunt. advince would at the most give them
lld. per ton, whilst the wale:miters would tell
their customers that in consequence of the advance
they would require from Is. to 2s. per ton advance.
The men have set, their leaders at defiance, and
there are at least the men employed at nearly 26 -
of the largest collieries in Yorkshire in open revelt
against them. Meetings have been held, and int
several cases the men have agreed to limit the
output of coal to less than one half of what haa
bten recently raised, so us to compel their employers
to give. what they want.

articles.title: I)liliiikl4.
articles.text:
I)liliiikl4.

A meeting of mittens in connection with the
Durham Atinera° Union was held on Saturday at
Durham. Between thirty and forty thousand,
miners were present. The secretary stated that ihk
the last twelve months the number of members had
increased from two thousand to thirtty-twob
thousand, and the funds in hand from a iew tutu
&ads to upwards of nine thousand pound. Reso-
lutions wore adopted urging the Governmen.t ta
secure the passing of the Mines Regulation Bill in
tho shape in which it has been introduced, and
affirming the importance of arbitration for settling
differences between employer and employed.

DIMONSTILATION OP 3IINHIIB IN IitTRIIAIt.

A demonstration, unparalleled in its signiiicana,
unapproached in numerical strength, and of
undoubted importance to the whole mining com-
munity of this country was held on Durham Race-
course on Saturday. The outing was arranged
under the auspices of the Durham County Miners'
Association, and it was rendered all the mom
enjoyable, perhaps, on account of the really re-
markable prosperity which has of late attended the
operations of that body. Some idea may be formed
ail to the imposing character of the spectaFle and
the importance attached to it, from the fact that
upwards of seventy immense silk banners had been
specially designed and emblazoned for the event.
Many of these wore extremely handsome in
design—not unfrequently bearing well-painted
scenes and figares—and many others owed not
little of their beauty and attractiveness to .the
gorgeous trimmings and tassels with which they
eteisrttasi. T

articles.title: AGMOULTURAL LABOURERS'
articles.text:
THE AGMOULTURAL LABOURERS'

MOVEMENT.

orEN-AIR MEETINa AT cHAiti).

The movement for increasing the wages of farm
labourers reached Chard on Friday evening. The
town had been posted will bills, announcing that
Mr. George Potter and Mr. George 11Iitchell, of
London, would address a meeting, with others.
The meeting was held in the open space close to
the South-Western Railway Station, the speakers
occupying a platform inside the railings of the
field adjoining the road. There was a very large
attendance—estimated at between 2,000 and 3,000,
the majority being of the labouring classes. A
number of farmers were also present. The proceed-
ings throughout were very orderly.
Upon the motion of the Rev. S. Walmsley,
seconded by Mr. Mitchell, Mr. George Potter was
voted to the chair.

The Chairn3an opened the proceedings in a
speech which dealt with the question from the
economical point of view, and showed to the evi-
dent conclusion of those present that the labourers
wore greatly underpaid. The chairman stated that
only two members of Parliament had been asked to
attend the meeting—both of whom expressed
sympathy with the objects of the meeting—the

Hon. Auberon Herbert, member for Nottingham,
and Mr. H. James, Q.C., member for Taunton.
Mr. James writes as follows :

"23, Wilton-place, Juno 11, 1872.
"DrAu Stn,—My Piirliamentary and profes-
sional duties press so heavily upon me that it la
quite impossible to attend at Chard on Friday next.
My absence, however, will in no way proceed from
want of sympathy with a properly conducted
movement on the part of the poor agricultural
labourers.—l am, 4e.,
"U. JAMES."
(Cheers.)

The Hon. Auboron Herbert writes:—

11.1 Y DEAIt Sllt,-" I ern very sorry not to be
able to be with you on Friday. Please express
my regtet that I cannot be so. I hope that the
men will act with moderation in word and deed,
but still be resolute in forming a union.

The Rev Canon Girdlestone writes to the effect
that he has other meetings vrhichhe is compelled
to attend, and cannot therefore be present.
I will now ask you to listen to one who was an
agricultural labourer, who is a native of this
county, and who takes considerable interest in
this movement, lie and I were at Montacute a
fortnight ago. The labourers there, I understand,
have had their wages raised from 10s. to 12s. a
week. (Cheers.) So, you see, our coining down
has done some good to the men of Montacute, who
never knew wages so high. Suite of you may
have experience of it before this day fortnight. I
now beg to introduce—Mr. George Mitchell, who
is styled as " One from the Plough." (Cheers,)
Mr. George Mitchell, having alluded to his
knowledge of the plough, then said that he would
read them a letter; it was as follows :

Athenteum Club, June sth, 1872.

challenge you to a disouAsion on the
wag,s question of agricultural labourers, when
and where you please ía Wiltshire or (.41 ueester-
shire. A letter sent to the Post Office, (thelien-
barn, will meet with prompt atteuti on. L. C. J.
Wulsey.
Ho had answered this letter as follows :

Sin,— I will take your challenge for £lOO. If
you van show that the labourers of Montaeute are
well paid you shall be the winner, and if I can
show that they too badly paid I shall be the
winner. (I did not omit to put in that. Laughter.)
The money to be given to the poor people who
used to tollow the plough with me at Montaeute.
(Cheers.) The meeting to take place on the 15th
of this month at half-past six o'clock—you paying
half and I the other half of the expenses of
getting up the meeting. An answer by return will
oblige, sours faithfully,

-ONE FROM TILE PLOUGH.

He had heard nothing of the reply. Mr. Wolsey
could not answer, as be supposed the challenge was
a little too hot for him. He also stipulated that
the farmers and labourers of Montacute should
decide the challenge, and he knew pretty well
what the decision would be. He had been away
from the autigh twenty-seven years. He could
remember when be had no hat, (Laughter.) Did
they think that he bud any glister motivesin coming
amongst theca ? (No, no.) Not long since an
honourable and rev. Doctor of Divinity told the

laboureiriat Leatnington, in Warwickshire, that he
did not see why the labourers there should make a
fuss when the labourers in the west were working for
Bs. a week. Was that true? (Voices: That's right.)
He (Mr. Mitchell) would inform them that they
bad not had Bs. a week long. (Voices: "Four
shillings in the winter.") Their wages had not
averaged 7s. a week when loss of time was taken
into account. (Cheers.) If they remained at

home of a rainy day their masters, as a rule, did
not pay them for that day. (Shame.) When he
read the doctor's speech, he felt insulted that
while the men in the north earned 163., the men
in the west were paid but 7s. he was determined
to stand this no longer, and resolved to make a
move at all costs, and there ho was. (Loud
cheers.) If any commercial man, in his commer-
cial capacity, had anything to say against him,
let him say it. He, having got good himself,
wished to do good to others. (Cheers.) But he
had not attained to his present position without
great difficulty. When he left home he was
unable to road or write, and he could not there-
fore write to the young lady whom be had left
behind at Montacuto. That was no credit
to the farmers. Ho had heard that there
were some very kind farmers in that neigh-
bourhood, and be would give all honour
to them. He was not there to set thorn fighting
with their masters, but merely to ask them to
reason with those masters, and to tell them that
they (the labourers) did not get so many mutton
chops as they would like. (Laughter, and a voice
—" And Writ going to, neither.") When ho first
went to London he was a perfect stranger, and
they told him that he was so remarkably green that
he had run away from the country because the
cows should not eat him. (Loud laughter.) He
believed there was a great deal of truth in it. He
was unable to read the names of the streets, and
feared that there were many not much better off
now. (Laughter and hear, hear.) He fell in with
a Sunday school teacher, who asked him to attend
the school. Ho consented, and was directed to
teach some of the youngest children their lessons.
He got on very well for a time, but at last ho came
to a word which the children could not spell. They
appealed to him, and he, of course, could not help
them. The whole school was looking at him, and
ho was in a dilemma. He said to them several
times, "Come, you must spell this." But they
failed, and he added, "What dunces you are."
At length the thought struck him to turn the
book and appeal to some of the other children, who
of course, spelt the word at once. (Laughter.)
He was not caught in that way a second time.
That was the commencement of his education,
and of his prosperity. (Cheers.)
,If there
were a farmer present be would like to ask
him if he had not often seen the little
bird-keeping boys in the fields " furridg-
ing " about the roots of the trees in the hedges.
They were looking for snails to roast fur their
dinners. ! Alt ! and cries of" Shame.") Did
they think that that was not a fact? It was true,
for be had dune so many a time himself, and that
in a Christian land. ("Shame.") Was it not dune
now? Yes, and with no credit to the farmers.
He then described the dinner provided by his
mother when his father earned only Bs. a week.
It N 1 as a kind of soup, composed of tail corn,
treacle and salt. Another dish consisted of potatoes
fried in bacon fat. Ho had received a letter signed
by R. Donne, Esq. containing the assertion that
the labourers earned ss, a day. To that he gave
the lie direct. There was not a farmer present who
ever paid his men ss. a day. They used to say,
" Those who ask for it shall not have it, and those
who don't ask don't want it." He supposed that
that was the case with many before him. They
did not want any increase of wages because they
had not asked for it, and if they asked they would
get the " sack. " (" That's it, sir, " and cheers.)
A gentleman wrote to him in London, and said,
" Ah, you are pigheaded! The farmers won't dine
with you at the club this year!" Ho bad not done
anything to the farmers. He was the best
man living with the farmers about three
months ago. How was it that he had
become so black ell at once ? Because
he t dcl the farmers that they bad a duty
to do, and they did not like to hear it or to do it.
(Loud cheers.) And as the farmers would not do
it, he asked the labourers to do it for them.
This, however, was impossible unless they com-
bined. He came there to assist them to combine,
and for that ho was branded as a rascal. He
then alluded to the argument that the farmers
could not afford to give higher wages, and stated
that not six months ago a farmer told him that he
was prepared to stake £lOO that he could produce
80 tons of tnangold wurtzel an acre from a piece
of land in his occupation. Farmers realised good
prices for their butter, which was from Is. 41. to
Is. 6d. a lb., and bread was 61d, a loaf. in London

they paid 71d., but frequently had a piece over.
Was the bread weighed in Chard? (No, no.)
He hoped that that fact would reach the ears of
some one in authority, 'who would see that the
bread t 9 tho poor was supplied by weight. He
gave a copy of the union rules to a farmer when

coming down in the train. The farmer said," Are
you peop!o °lining down here to kick up a noise?
I don't know that you will be allowed to hold
your meeting." (Laughter.) At all events
the meeting was held. The labourers saw
the sheep running about the fields, but that
was all the share they had. (A, voice—" We can
hardly catch hold of their tails." Laughter.)

In some things a look was of value. But it was
another thing to look at a good supper and go
without one. Beef and mutton averaged loa. a

lb. for good joints. What, therefore: had the
farmers to complain of? Every kind of produce
was selling well, and they ought not to grumble
because the labourers asked for a little extra. It
had been stated that he (tr. Mitchell) pocketed
the money collected for strikes. He should like
some of those who spoke in that way to have bad
his pocket during the past month. He mould
guarantee that they would have scratched their
heads. (Laughter.) He admired the man who
strived to keep out of the workhouse. It showed
that he had an English heart within him. Local
boards and common councilmen ought to efl.
courage the man who endeavoured to keep himself
out of the union. If a fair day's work was
to be got out of a man he ought to have
some beef steaks, which they would find was
much better than what was known as " ilippit."
(Laughter.) He remembered that one of the
best men who ever worked upon Abbey
Farm, Montaeute, had only Bs. a-week. That
man, when he put in his sickle, cut almost a sheaf
at every stroke. What was he receiving now?
Eighteenpence and a loaf. (" Shame.") Out of
which be had ls. a week house rent to pay.
(Renewed cries of "shame.") How much butcher's
meat could that poor fellow have ? Could be get
bread? Nay, could he get " taties and rah ?" If
they were to visit his home what would they see ?
(Voices: "Poverty.") Ile was not an old man/
just over sixty, but worn out. He never left his
house without tAking the key with him for fear
that anyone should see its wretched contents. His
furniture and everything he possessed, if brought
to the hammer, would not realise 2s. That was
only one case. He could give other cases as bad.
(Sensation.) That poor fellow was literaliy
starving. If any medical gentlemen were present,
he would- ask them to give truthful certiticams,
and not, when a man was starved to death, certify
that he died from natural causes. The effect of
their combining would be that the masters would
be all the better for having better men. They
would get more work done, more good looks, and
there would not be so many people speaking
against them. If the labourers were fed anti
clothed well, they would take pride in their homes,
iodyi ireot of
supposelabr
as
iou
and would be happier altogether. He had to
doubt
y fthaatriluieer
in Cabs
alrad, furrgeanheem
that one of them had ever employed 500 men at
one time. (Voices : "Not five.") The labourers
were deserving of an increase, they ought to have
it, and they should have it. (Loud cheers.)
Mr. James Male proposed the following resolu-
tion, which was road by the Chairman :

"Resolved, that this meetiug (loop] y sympathises
With the long deproisod condition of the agri-
cultural 14bouiers of Sqinersetshire and approves
of the estabiklininit 0f a branch of the N thou al
Agricultural Libourers' Union at Chard for the
rurpose of improving the condition of the labourer,
snit the labourers present pledge themselves to be-
come members of the union, and to use every effort
to induce other labourers to do likewise." (Cheers.)
Mr. John Beavis seconded the resolution.
The Rev. S Walinsley supported the resolution.
lie had for many years done a little in divinity,
and thought it now high time to do something
in morals. He asserted that the agricultural
labourers of Somerset could not be honest with the
pay they received. Some said that, as a minister,
he was isolated in that movement. Such was not
the case. The Rev. C. H. Spurgeon wrote to the
ehairman", at Montacute sympathising with the
objects of the meeting, and expressed a hope that
the labourers of Somerset would soon be delivered
from the land of bondage. (Cheers.) Dr. Watts,
many years ago, put into rhyme the followiug
The softened ridges of the field
Permit the corn to spring,
The vall.,ys rich profusion yield.,
And the poor labourers sing.

" Tho valleys rich profusion yield." But for
whom? For someboly ? Not for the labourer,
who had to sing the doxology of praise for sending
the farmer health and riches. But there were
better days in store for the labourers, who
ought to have 15s. or 16s. ft week. It
woull make them happier and better

citizens, and more honest. Could a man
satisfy the demands of his constitution with Bs. a
week? Nbver. Could he answer the great pur-
pose for which he was created? Never. A man
bad not only to be fed, but his mind required
cultivation. Had the lthourer money to lay out
in education? He left them to Answer the
question. He had visited many of the labourers'
houses in Dorset, and had askel for their libraries.
They replied that they had none. They had not
time to read books. He bad often lamented their
condition, and expressed the hope that some one
would be raised up to defend the cause of the men
and bring their wretched condition before the
publie.
The resolution was carried unanimously.

The Chairman asked the labourers to leave their
names at the Rev. Mr. Walmsley's residence, and
they would at once be formed into a union. Ho
explained the rules, and urged all to join. He did
uot suppose that they would be required to strike
in that locality, for the farmers woul I be sure to
meet them fairly. If they joined the union, how-
ever, they would not be at the mercy of the ftrruers
or landowners. In his experience he found that em-
ployers- were no worse off for giving good wages
to their men. Working men formed the pedestal
of society, and if tney were raised those who stood
upon their shoulders must be raised also. Ad he
Wished was, that the property of the country should
be more et-pally divided. If the result was that
the men received a little more wages, the country
would be benefited, and he should not regret his
visit to Chard.

The Rev. S. Wa'lnsley proposed a vote of thanks
to t le Chairman, Mr. Mitchell, and to the reporters.
(Cheers.)
Cheers were given for the union and for the
farmers who paid the highest wages, and the meet-

The strike at Cubbington, Weston, Lining-
ton, Offoliurch, and Ilunningham still con—
tinues, and the area will this week be
enlarged; the labourers of Whitn ash and Bishop's
Teachbroolco have given notice that in future they
shall require the union terms, both as to wriges,
hours and overtime. A stalk° has also occurred
at Luddington, near Stratford-on-Avon, and Bide-
ford, near Alcester. Six 1 ibourers from Ludding-
ton were on Friday charged at the Stratford
County Petty Sessions with threatening Isaac
Bennett, in the employ of Messrs. William and
Edward Boddington, at Luddington. AU the
summonses were dismissed, except one against
Isaac Bennett, who was cent to goal fur 21 days.
The ease for the prosecution was that when Davis
went to take the place of a man on strike, Ben-
nett and six others went down and threatened
"what they would do" if ho did not leave work.
There are probably now about 500 men on strike
in Warwickshire. Large union meetings still
continue to be held, and the number of unionists
is reported to be steadily inereasing.

articles.title: GLOUCEbTER.
articles.text:
GLOUCEbTER.

The West of England Labourers' Union,
now bein4 nrmed in Gloucestershire and else.
where, is making rapid progress. A large
meeting was held late on Monday night, on a
green by the road-side, in the village of Staunton,
between Gloucestershire and Worcestershire.
Many of the labourers' wives were present with
them. It was stated that in the group of villages
of which Staunton is the centre there are now
nearly 200 members, all of whom have paid their
entrance fees, and were keeping up their payments.
One of the men who spoke, a carpenter, sketched
out a Republican scheme, under which the
labourers were peaceably to MtlS3 together their
funds, and therewith buy back and fairly distribute
the large tracts of land that had, he said, centuries
ago unfairly come into the hands of their present
posseasors. This scheme, however, did not accon

with the views of his bearers, and the urgent
advice of the succeeding speakers was to be
moderate, but firm.

TUE NATIONAL AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS' UNION.

A meeting of the National Agricultural
Labourers' Union was held on Tuesday (Mr.
Joseph Arch in the chair), at the Guernsey Tem-
perance Hotel, Leamington. Letters wore read
showing that nearly every county in England had
joined the Union, and that the members number
about 160,000. About a dozen organizing
lecturers were appointed to establish branches
in various districts in- England and Wales. The
terms of the Warwickshire Union are, it is stated,
to be insisted on throughout the country.
'Letters were received from the following, con-
senting to act on the Consultative Board:—Mr.
George Potter, Mr. Harry Duckett, Mr. Lloyd
Jones, Mr. J. A. Campbell, Professor Beesly,
Mr. E. Jenkins, Dr. Langford, Rev. O'Neil,
Canon Girdlestone, Mr. G. Dixon, M.P., Rev. F.
S. Attonborough, Mr. J. E. Cox, Mr. G. Dawson,
Hon. Auberon Herbert, Mr. G. Ward, Mr. S.
Morley, 1.1. P., Mr. Hodgson Pratt, Mr. Jesse
Collings, and Mr. A. Arnold. The replies con-
tained many expressions of good wishes for the
success of the union. The committee received
information of several acts of coercion and in.
thnidation on the part of employers, and directed
their solicitor to watch the cases, and take action
if considered desirable. The commiteee arranged
to hold their meetings on alternate Mondays.

MEETING. AT MONTACUTIt.

On Saturday evening about 400 labourers and
glove makers met in the Borough, Montacute, for
the purpose of hearing a report of the union formed
there a fortnight ago, and to correct some mis-
statements as to the earnings of the workpeople.
The electing was addressed. by Mr. George Potter,
of London, and by the "Man from the Plough "

(Mr. Mitchell), and others.
Mr. Mitchell said that Mr. IL Southcombe,
glove manufacturer, of Stoke, had published a
letter in the papers stating that "a young person
who works a whole week can earn from 7s. to 108.,
and sometimes more." He asked the glove
makers present if that was correct. They unani-
moway declared " No." He then asked what was
the average earnings? and the reply was that they
did not amount to more than 28. Gd. a week. Mr.
?slitehell then referred to a letter signed " Runty
Copper," in which the writer said that the

labourers of Mont:mute had meat every Sunday, as
any person could see who watched the "meat and
Sggicl puddings "that came from the bakehouse.
In answer to this Mr. Mitchell slid that two men
visited the two bakehouses on Sunday, and that at
one no labourer's dinner was to he fined, but that
at the other was one piece of meat in potatoes,
valued at 5d.; another, half a sheep's head, 4d.i
and two more—one being two pennyworth of
bullock's fat, and the other three half-pencn worth
of the sumac—the whole, including potatoes,
amounting to not more than 2s. So much for the
statement of "Army Cupper," who is supposed to
have been dead 20 years. Evidence of the dinners

(the speaker said) could he given by the owners of
the bakehouses. Mr. Mitchell then tefurred to
the tyranny of some farmers who had discharged
labourers, the names of whom the secretary, Mr.

IVESTEItHAIS, KENT.

On Wednesday evening last, an open-air meet-
ing was hold in the maiket-place in order to form
a branch of the National Agricultural Labourers'
Union. Being market-day there was a good
attendance of farmers, besides some seven or
eight hundred labourers. Mr. White (butcher), of
Shoreham, was voted to the chair. After express-
ing his hearty zeal for the cause which bad
gathered them together, the chairman introduced
to the meeting Mr. J. Charles Cox, a Derbyshire
magistrate. Mr. Cox said that he had made the
acquaintance of the Kent delegates at the recent
,onterence of agricultural labourers at Leaming-
ton, and that as he was in the neig hbourhood and

regarded this movement as a national one, he had
willingly assented to Speak to them On the advan-
tages of union. The miaerablcinsuftWenny of
labourers wages had been fully shown in the Blue
Books on the Employment of Women and
Children in Agriculture, and he had, moreover, a
practical acquaintance with their too often
wretched condition. Ho did not attribute that
condition near so much to the individual caprice
or tyranny of particular landlords or farmers, as
to the state of our land laws, which had been
gradually bringing matters to their present
plight; and to the merciless way in which class
legislation had robbed them'of their commons.
Mr. Gilham, a labourer of Oxford, supported
the formation of a branch of the National Union
at Westerham, in an able and energetic speech,
and many others gave their experiences of want
and suffering.
