FRIDAY, JUNE 21, 1872.

THE BUILDERS' STRIKE AND LOCK-

OUT.

THE effect of a strike is so obvious to every
mind, and presses so heavily upon those who
have to share among themselves the cost of it,
that only very silly and superficial people can
run away with the notion of intelligent work-
ing men having any delight in such an ex-
pedient. Two weeks' pay has now been
handed over to the three hundred men who
have desisted from work at two building
firms. The sum of these payments proves,
indeed, the determination of men in the same
trade to support eaeh other; but it also shows
that measures of so expensive a kind
cannot very long be persisted in. The
numerous public who speak without thinking,
and judge without investigation, may be in-
duced to take up the cry of "This is the
consequence of trades unions ;" but the truth
is, as every observer at once intelligent and
unprejudiced, must perceive and be persuaded,
that all concerned in the matter, masters and
men, and those the meeting of whose require-
ments depends upon smooth working betwixt
employers and employed, owe more to trades
unions than to any other persons or things,
on account of the steady tendency of such
combinations, under the direction and with
the support of cool-headed and sober-minded
men, to diminish as far as possible the temp-
tation to strikes and the impulse to lock-outs,
and to turn all points of dispute between those
who work and those who hire into the safe
and reasonable channel of conciliation and
arbitration.

Outside judges do not always bear in mind
the inside difference between a strike of men
and a lock-out by masters. A strike may be
,justifiable or unjustifiable, or, if the latter,
it may have more or less to say for itself. It
must, at any rate, commend itself to those on
whom it retires for support. But a lock-out
is the severest form of refusal that can be con-
ceived. In the judgment of those against
whom the blow is directed, it is might against
right; and, if objectors urge that those who
strike or who support a strike, are not neces-
sarily always in the right, why, even then, a
lock-out in answer to a strike assumes the yet
more odious form of the strong against the
weak, than which, reduced to a general
proposition, and stripped, of all special
attributes, the mind of man and human ex-
perience know nothing more oppressive or
more condemnable.

If men and masters could heartily unite in the
view, that to call in foreign arbitrators is to cast a
slur on both parties, as if incapable of settling
their own trade differences among themselves,
pure conciliation might be hopefully attempted
—conciliation which, as all must admit, is better
than arbitration under any form. But con-
ciliation, by itself alone, is apt to fail ;
and frequent experience has pointed out
the expediency, as it has borne witness to
the success, of codes of regulations under which
conciliation and arbitration are embraced in
one scheme, the second as a suecedaneum to
the first. Nobody, in fine, can be surprised at
the men distrusting either a scheme of arbitra-
tion, which would refer the questions in dispute
to a numerous board, or one which, while com-
prising them to a few, would select the
individuals without reference to special know-
ledge of trade matters or to skilled experience
in handling them. The best thing would be
for the masters to endeavour to bring them-
selves and each other to simple compliance with
the claims of the men; the next best thing,
the
for masters gucl wen W place themselves

hands, either of one man, such as Mr.
RUPERT KETTLE, or for each party to select an
arbitrator, and leave these two, if found
necessary, to call in an umpire, having the
confidence of them both.

Until this is done there remains nothing
except to await the issue and see which side
can stand out longest. The men are acting
entirely within their rights. They say we see
a good chance of getting the terms we want;
we believe they are no more than we deserve,

articles.title: LITTLE BIRDS AND THEIR PERSECUTORS.
articles.text:
THE LITTLE BIRDS AND THEIR
PERSECUTORS.

THE working men of our towns are not as
a rule active destroyers of small birds, but,
nevertheless, we are anxious to back the
plea for mercy put in on the birds' behalf.
There are large numbers of animals doomed by
man to destruction by habit and necessity. For
these nothing need be said, as anything that
could be urged would avail little. But the
small birds, who give us so much and take
from us so little, ought to be spared. We love
the fields and the woods the better because
they are the habitations of birds.
Hail, old patrician trees, so great and good!
Hail, ye plebeian underwood:
Where the poetic birds rejoice,
And for their quiet nests, and plenteous food,
Pay with their grateful voice.

We do not desire to :interfere with sport,
but the man who seeks for it by shooting the
thrush, the blackbird, the lark, the robin, or
our familiar little impudent acquaintance, the
sparrrow, cannot have any great sense of
the beautiful in him, and certainly must
be untroubled by the stirrings of pity.
We are bound to thank the Baroness COUTTS
for her merciful remonstrance. And we ought
to be grateful to AUBERON HERBERT for point-
ing out the usefulness of our little friends, the
small birds. Such considerations, however,
can hardly be expected to influence the
heartlesasavage
,or thoughtless oaf who goes
out with his gun to murder our little feathered
musicians. We should like very much to see
their time and their ammunition employed on
larger and less lovely game. Lucfax's
Lachanopteri, a large wonderful fowl with
great bunches of cabbages instead of wings,
would be a capital bird for these sportsmen
to take home to feed their young on. Or
some of those birds mentioned in the
" Talmud," one of which, when standing
standing in a river, the waters of which only
reached to the lower joint of its leg; yet the
river was so deep that a carpenter's axe thrown
in did not find the bottom in seven years. A
handsome sum of money might be made by
shooting one of these, and sending a leg to
the British Museum. We are informed, too,
in the same book that a Rabbi saw a flock of
geese in a desert, whose feathers were forced
off by their fat, and whose wings and
legs wore intended for food in Paradise.
How much better than a robin would one of
these be. Sir John MAUNDEVILLE speaks of
a very curious sparrow-hawk in "Little
Emory" which it would be a blessing to get
rid of. SINBA.D'S Roo could hardly be missed if
fired at with ordinary skill, and although we
are not informed what the flesh is like, there
cannot be much doubt that those who fed on
him might cut and come again. There would
be no use in sending our sportsmen after the
Porphyrion, as:that bird was long ago de-
stroyed by women, for discovering their in-
fidelity to their husbands. They might, ho w-
aver, have a shot at the Merops, which flies
backward, tail first; such an absurd animal
deserves no quarter.

In fact, we should liko to see these bird-
killers employed in any kind of useful way.
To teach them lessons of humanity seems a
hopeless task ;—to restrain them by law almost
as hopeless,with such lawmakers as we have got.
What a blessing, therefore, it would be could
we persuade them to betake themselves to the
wilderness in search of those fat geese seen
long ago by the Rabbi—if, for no other
reason, in the hope they might stay there for
ever to feed on that oily fowl.

articles.text:
MILITARYISM.

IVEnt: we to ask ourselves what, at the
present moment, was the great universal
thought of the civilized world, the reply, if an
honest one would have to be "Militaryism."
The arts and industrial occupations have
an interest to individuals and to classes ; the
organization of armies and navies is the
thought of Governments, and is, therefore,
necessarily forced into the minds of all men;
for all have to serve, or in some way pay for
such service. In France at present this
thought is most active, and although •M.
Trims differs from many of those around
him as to method, there is no difference as to
object. We are also trying to re-model our
Army, and the last report from America spoke
of the strengthening of coast defences. To the
world generally, it does not matter whether
M. THEIRS and his ministers, or their oppo-
nents in the Chamber, succeed, in any case
war is the outlook. In fact, the intellect
of the present hour is at work to find out how
best to make war, not do discover how most
effectually to promote and preserve peace.
How to kill men, destroy villages, towns and
cities, lay waste fields, is the most universal
thought among statesmen.
The managers of nations, having made their
preparations, will, as a matter of course, make
occasions to test them. Secret diplomacy
furnishes such opportunities. The Emperor
of FRANCE sent a messenger to the King of
PRUSSIA, and immediately after the demon of
war broke loose to afflict the world with
horror. We do not know at what moment
some blundering treaty-maker may land us in
a like moss. The Throne, which means the
Administration, can declare war at any
moment without consulting the people; and
the nation must find money and men if defeat
and disgrace are to be prevented. Is it not,
therefore, worth while to make open diplomacy
a popular question? The QUEEN and her
Ministers, and all other potentates and their
advisers, are clever and respected persons,
but the game they are playing is a tremendous
one in its consequence, and those who have
to pay the stakes should have sometning to
say as to its conditions before they sit
down to it. The people of different countries
are growing faster in mutual trust than
governments are; a sense of mutual respect
and a desire for common guarantees of
peace exist more strongly amongst them
than amongst the rulers of nations. It is not
too much to say that if that little game at
Washington, conducted so blunderingly by our
diplomatic sachems and sagarnores, had from
the first been understood by the nation and
made the subject of ordinary criticism, the
present misunderstanding would, ten to one,
have been avoided.

We do not desire to quarrel with the
American people, and it is just as certain they
do not want to go to war with Us. Amongst
the masses of the people on both sides, it would
be difficult to imagine any difference that could
lead to such a thing. But, notwithstanding
this, the sachems and sagamores are moving
us along quite naturally, and in their old way
in that direction. There are men on both
sides who would welcome a war because they
would profit by it. Statesmen have been
known to precipitate wars for the purpose of
covering blunders for which they expected to
be called to account. But the people can never
have an interest in such national madness.
Peace is and ever must be best in every way
for them. And if they would have it pre-
served, they must exercise a direct and strong
control over such negociations es have a
tendency either to preserve or disturb it.

articles.title: HOUSE OF LORDS AND THE
articles.text:
THE HOUSE OF LORDS AND THE

BALLOT.

Tut,: Duke of RICHMOND, as leader of the
Opposition in the House of Lords, has verified
the expectation that, though ho discreetly re-
commended the second reading of the Ballot
Bill, he would take care to make up in com-
mittee for his forbearance at the previous
stage. His series of amendments began at
the second clause. The first was that the
Ballot papers should be numbered and attached
to counterfoils bearing the same numbers; the
returning officer printing on the counterfoil the
voter's nuraber in the register. The argument

was, that the means of scrutiny were needful to
prevent or punish personation, and the plea for
the particular method was, its alleged corres-
pondence to a provision in the Marquis of
HARTINGTON9S last year's Bill. The answer of
Lord RIPON rested upon the partiality of this
selection from that measure, which contained
many provisions to preserve secrecy which
his Grace had taken care to omit. For the rest,
to first accept a Bill and then nullify
its chief purport, was an unworthy proceeding,
and a merely optional ballot would be worth-
less against intimidation. Lord CAIRNS en-
deavoured to separate the considerations
embraced by the PRESIDENT of the CouNcrL
and to confine attention to that which
affected to be wholly bent upon preventing
personation of voters by fraudulent individuals.
As the LOUD CHANCELLOR showed, however,
the series of amendments which. the Duke of
RICHMOND had put upon the paper, were
evidently so contrived as to lead by steps to
one sure effect, disclosure of every man's vote.
Moreover, the first of those did not afford the
means of detecting personation on the spot,
while it would open the door to a system of
intimidation. Nevertheless, the amendment
was carried by a majority of 162 to 91.
This insidious attack upon the principle of
the Bill was immediately followed up by an
open thrust at its very life. Availing himself
of the plea that, as the measure came
up from the Commons, it invaded
secrecy by allowing the presiding officer to
help men unable to write in filling up their
paper in the presence of the electionering
agents, the DuKE produced his second amend-
ment with the observation that this invasion
would be carried no further by leaving it at
the option of voters to retire or not to retire
into the private box to mark and fold their
papers. Lord RIPON met this pretence by
declaring his readiness to omit the clause
respecting official help to unlettered voters.
The Marquis of SALISBURY twitted the friends
to the measure in the House of Commons
with the erasure of the penal clauses, and
argued in his usual way for optionality,
arguments quite superfluous on his own
showing; namely, that, if the Bill passed in
its original form, he could undertake to
ascertain, if he wanted to know, how every
tenant on his estate voted. Lord LYTTLETON
'gave the Opposition a rebuke the more pointed
as coming from no friend to the measure. He
would not vote, he said, for an amendment the
object of which was to reduce to nullity a
Bill allowed to pass its second reading. An
optional ballot, as Lord KIMBELEY contented
himself with remarking, was no ballot at all
while, as Lord GRANVILLE justly added, the
amendment under consideration was at utter
variance with the pretended wish to give pro-
tection to those who desired it. But what is
the use of argument, however oonolusive, in
the face of a majority who have made up their
minds to effectually destroy the measure
which they first affected to accept. This also,
and the other amendments ef which the Duke
of Rion atoND had given notice, were easily •
carried.

Of the other amendments proposed,and either
accepted or rejected, one only needs to be
described here—that, namely, of Earl &urns-
BURY, who, at the request, as he stated, of a
large deputation of working men, moved two
clauses, the first to keep open polls from eight
to eight, the second to close public-houses
during the polls. The first was opposed
by both the Marquis of RIPON and Lord
CA.TuNs ; yet, on a division, was carried
by a majority of 17 (89 to 72). "The result,"
it is stated by the reporter, "appeared greatly
to astonish the House." And, in fact, it led to
an altercation such as, for warmth, is not often
seen in the House of Lords. Lord CAIRNS
sharply upbraided "the spokesman of the
Government" with having distinctly led the
House to suppose that Ministers and their sup.
porters were going to oppose the clause, and '
yet, at the last moment, and after the division
had been called, they went into the lobby with
the noble EARL. To this complaint, however,
Earl Grt.trimix had a clear answer. Had the
Opposition, he suggested, been in the least
degree aware that the Government were going
to support the clause extending the hours of
polling, that would have been reason enough

with noble Lords opposite, in favour of the
proposal, to forego their personal convictions
and unite in a prrty vote. What Lord RIPoN
had done was, to express regret that
the proposal had not been adopted by
the House of Commons, and to recommend
Lord SHAFTESBURY to bring up his clause in
a somewhat amended form on the report.
That noble EARL, instead of taking the advice,
insisted upon dividing; and therefore, Lord
RIPON was not chargeable with any inconsis-
tency in following him into the lobby. The
Duke of RICHMOND and his friends were des-
perately annoyed at this unexpected improve-
ment of the Bill, which it was their solo
object to emasculate; and, for the opportunity
thus afforded to working men to vote at
elections, they took a characteristic revenge
by giving a majority of 90 (133 to 43), ia
favour of keeping open publiohouses during all
the hours of polling. Another new clause,
moved by Lord BEAUCHAMP, and carried by a
majority of 37 (106 to 69), will, if agreed to
by the Commons, limit the duration of the
Act to the year 1880. As the third reading
may take place to-day, we shall soon know
which amendments the Commons agree to,
and from which they dissent. At any rate,
the Ballot is now carried.

IMPRISONMENT FOR SMALL DEBTS.

Mn. BASS'S Bill for the Abolition of Impri-
sonment for Small Debts has been lost in the
House of Commons. This is another instance of
the disgraceful indifference with which ques-
tions are treated which only aired a circum-
scribed number of poor and suffering people in
the People's House. Let the public think of
the fact that men are sent to prison by the
Judges ot our County Courts for is. 10d. Such
a proceeding would be a disgrace to the most
illiterate and malignant tribe of savages. The
breadwinner of a family looked up for fourteen
days for a debt of is. 10d. is a fact as stupid
as it is wicked.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL sighed over the
matter, and said it was lamentable, but he
preferred slowness, lest, perhaps, the change
peoposed should bring down the whole fabrio
of constitutional law. He preferred, on the
whole, to wait. So did the House, and, there-
fore, decided, by 136 against 34, that nothing
should be done.

Mr. BASS, however, must not despair. If
public attention can be called to this iniquity,
the House of Commons, in fear of this, will
some day vote more in accordance with uom
mon humanity and common sense; meantime,
certain numbers of poor families will be
ruined, but that is not much, except to those
who suffer the ruin; and these, as a rule, are
an unsavoury lot, justifying, no doubt, in the
House of Commons, the conclusion of TENNY.
sox's Secbnd Northern Farmer, that "the
poor in a loomp is bad."

articles.title: GREAT TOWN SEWAGE WES-
articles.text:
THE GREAT TOWN SEWAGE WES-

TION.

SURELY one effect of Sir ROBERT PEEL'S
triumph in Parliament will be a more sensible
arrangement respecting matters so important
as providing for a safe, if not a useful, outflow
of the sewage of our great towns. He got rid
of the Birmingham Bill, for the moment, but
only by a majority of three in a House of three
hundred members. It was not likely that
the case should be otherwise. In a legislative
chamber so strongly interested in the main-
tenance of what landlords fancy to be their
rights, it could not but be that many Members
would sympathise with Sir ROBERT; but the
fact that a fair moiety of those present voted
the other way, must have served to convince
him and them, that the claims of the popula-
tion at large are paramount to those of any of
its mere portions or sections, and to the
rights, real or imaginary, of the least
numerous class. The banter and the
exaggeration spoken on the occasion will go
for nothing: A question truly national and
pressingly important waits to be decided; and
two things are quite certain—first, that it
cannot be settled by a series of private Bills ;
secondly, that it cannot be determined by
private interests, but must be considered
and concluded on the widest public grounds.

HISTORY OF THE INDIRECT CLAIMS.
Tim sPecial correspondent of the Daily

Now: at Geneva has clearly explained, and
with apparent truth, the origin of the "indirect
claims" as included in the American Case.
Mr. BANcaorr DANIS was called upon by the
Government at Washington to draw up that
document. Before he had completed the work,
claims poured in from citizens, not only for
actual losses, but also for increased rates of
insurance on ships and cargoes. The question
arose how such claims were to be treated. At
a consultation of the whole Cabinet it was
decided to admit them; but Mr. BA.Ncnorr
DAVIS was to include them in such a manner
that it should be impossible for the arbitrators
to award any pecuniary damages against Great
Britain upon them. This, it was considered,
would be achieved, by not giving the arbitra-
tors any data on which to award a sum of
money; whereas the direct claims were all
supplemented by elaborate statements, every-
thing expended or lost being set down to a
cent. The Washington Cabinet hoped that
ours would accept this scheme as a means of
obtaining a "lull, perfect, and final settle-
ment of all claims."

articles.title: PAYMENT OF WAGES BILL.
articles.text:
PAYMENT OF WAGES BILL.

THE Payment of Wages Bill has not met
with much favour in the House of Commons.
Such a measure is more than any other a test
of the good-will and practical fitness of our
legislators to deal with working men's ques-
tions. This question of " Truck" is not
political—not a matter of Conservative and
Liberal contention. It is purely a question
as between employer and employed, between
the interest of the men and their employers;
and when the test of practical legislation was
applied in the House the working men went
to the wall.

Every allowance shoull be made for the
crotchets of an honest man like Mr. FA.wcErr.
Us has got a principle astride of his shoulders
which rides him hard occasionally, and forces
him tomtit-nes into strange places. Nor do
we wish to be angry with Mr. POWELL. Tie
is a lawyer, and depends much for his position
on West Riding manufacturers. The brief ho
holds COMM from them, and his share in the
business was a matter of course. There is no
occasion:to go into particulars; the measure
has been shaped to suit the convenience of the
employers, and the men, as usual, must do
the best they can.

What can be more clear than the proved
evils of " Truck ?" What can be more
fraudulent that its every-clay practices? And
how, it may be asked, can it be abolished if
opportunity is given to carry it on under all
sorts of colourable pretences? "Freedom of
contract" is a good thing, so is " self.
reliance," so is moonshine when there is no
gas, and it on be had. Mr. FawcErr no
doubt knows how to make his contracts with-
out 'being driven into a truck-shop for any
part of his income as Professor. If the college
authorities insisted on his taking a portion of
it out in bad tea and coffee, 25 per cent.
dearer than the best stufr could be obtained
for ready money, ho would very likely throw
up his professorship. But if Mr. FlafeETT
had nothing else to depend on, and if there
were sevtral half-starved professors, with
families wanting bread, ready to take the
job, he might throw freedom of contract
over his shoulder and. htiok to his profee-:
sional chair. Mr. PowELL, too, may not
care a button whether he gets his foe
on one day rather than on another
provided he does get it; but a poor working
man may find it very inconvenient to draw his
wages at distant intervals, or to draw them in
truck if he cannot wait. If a man earns his
wages every week, what possible claim can an
employer have to keep 25 per cent. of them in
his bands for any period over that time? Much
might be said of the power it gives the eta-
plo)er over the poor worker, and much might
be added as to the way this power is
frequently used. But it drives men to
credit, and, beyond all this, as a simple
matter of trade, the truck shop is enor-
mously profitable, and tolls in so many ways
so advantageously for the employer that there
is no wonder he should hold to it with great
strength of grasp.
Working men who have moved about the
country know how the thing works; unprao7

tical political economists do not ; whilst law-
yers, whose practice it is to plead, don't care.
Two hundred pounds spent weekly in a truck
shop amounts to ten thousand four hundred
pounds in the year, which, at 30 per cent.
and truck is never done under that—will yield
an annual profit of £3,120; and this can be
done on an invested capital of £5OO, as that
much spent in fixtures and stock, where the
custom is under control, and steady and re-
gnlar ia its character, will easily meet the
demands of such a trade. This is a profit, too,
which does not vary. The owner of the este).-
lishment fixes his prices; and whilst the profits
of his regular trade, where he has competitors
to fight with, may vary—hero everything
takes place precisely as he wills, and in no
other way. Besides, as the money he pays on
Saturday in wages is back to his counting-,
house on Monday through the " till " of his
shop, he has only to arrange that the credit
he gives to the customers in his regular trade
shall be a little shorter than that he takes
from the merchants who supply his truck shop
to make his truck business one of the safest
and most profitable things imaginable. The
"free contract," made by the workman in
such cases, is a contract to be robbed with his
eyes open; he makes it that he may not be
starved, and ho boars it, and groans under it,
though it is a chain that ties him almost in
spite of himself to his servitude.

Mr. Mixei . and the Government made their
little shabby compromises with those who
opposed the Bill, because no working man's
pressure can be put on them in the House of
Commons. Of course, the workers may bring
their power to bear when the oleotions are on.
But the usual cries will be got up, the gongs
of party will be beaten—loyalty to party will
be mouthed,—the friends of "truck" will slip
in, and the old game of plunder will go on. It
is not pleasant to be continually repeating
advice which is disregarded, but in this matter
we may hope the working men are really
beginning to bestir themselves, If they can
keep alive in their breasts the indignation of
to-day till the elections come round, and then
bring it down heavily on the heads of offenders,
they will soon work the reform they need on
this and other questions. But if, as is their
habit, they run like sheep after the tinklings
of the old bell-wethers, this and other abuses
from which they suffer will remain, not only as
oppressions and frauds, but as marks of a
degraded position—of an inferior caste.

articles.title: TUE BALLOT MANGLED.
articles.text:
TUE BALLOT MANGLED.

Tin; House of Lords has effectually de-
stroyed the Ballot Bill. It was not to be
expected that these who, though prohibited
by the Constitution from doing so, always
managed to influence the elections in their
own favour, would allow the electors to escape
their control.

It was natural enough that those wko hate
the Bill in the Lords should use the same
sort of slip-shod arguments we had got sick
of in the Commons; but what they have done
might as well have been done in silence.
For more than half a century honest men
have been trying to secure the chance of
giving an honest and independent vote for
English elections, and during the whole of
that time their efforts have been defeated
by fraudulent pretences. Lot it not be for-
gotten that those who have been most active
in coercion and corruption, have also been
the most determined and persistent in their
Opposition to the Ballot. Notoriously, open
voting has for any time in the history of
England been a scandal and a disgrace.
It has promoted a kind of vice not in accord-
ance with our national character, and for pur-
poses any honest man would blush to own.
The dirtiest page in our history might be
written out of our parliamentary election
inquiries, and what would greatly add to the
rascality of its details is that these inquiries
were for the most part conducted with solemn
faces by men all of whom, or nearly all, were
themselves guilty of the practices they
enquired into with a view to their punish-
ment.

Let the working men of England remember
that our Parliament has its history; that our
elections did not begin this century; and that,
ever since they did begin, rich men have made

themselves richer by corrupting constituencies,
powerful men have grown stronger by control-
ling them. And everything that in our Go-
vernment militated against national liberty
or political honesty, has been fostered and
promoted by the rampant corruption, knavery,
and blackguardism, paid for by peers and rich
men, whenever a manageable constituency was
to be found, or wherever a sufficient number of
rogues could be bought to turn the scale in
favour of the rich and powerful corrupter.
In working this measure through the House
of Commons, logic or argument were not neces-
sary. These are only of use where men's
understandings are to be enlightened and
influenced; and after the debates of fifty
years nothing remained to be said that could
add force to what had already been said on
this subject. The honourable gentlemen on
one side of the House and the equally honour-
able gentlemen on the other, were simply con-
forming to habit by pelting each other with
words. Very few, even of the most Liberal,
desire the Ballot, simply because they know it
would limit the influence by which so many of
them found their way into the House. The
crowd of " honourable " roughs who dis-
tinguished themselves the other day by crow-
ing, and barking, and other farm-yard dis-
plays, could scarcely become members of a
deliberative assembly like the Commons House
of Parliament on their own merits. Every sen-
sible voter in the kingdom knows that a man
may crow excellently and bray as naturally
as the aldermen of Cervantes without being
fitted to make wise and useful laws. And
they know as well that the " ruck" of such
persons now in the House would not have been
there, were it not for the "influences," other
than legitimate ones, which can be brought to
bear for the purpose of forcing them on
the constituencies disgraced by sending them.
That the Lords should have the courage to
do what their friends and proteges in the
House of Commons only partly succeeded in
doing, ought to surprise nobody—can, in fad,
surprise nobody acquainted with the history
of our representative system. They have
made the Ballot Bill worth absolutely nothing,
and by so doing they have challenged the
nation to a trial of strength, and the
English people, particularly the working
men must take up their battle-gauge. Shall
rich gentlemen, with and without coronets,
dictate to the people of England the con-
ditions under which they shall reg ulate
their electoral proceedings, and shall they
be allowed to do so for the purpose
of retaining in their hands the old dishonest
power by which, in the past, they were '
enabled to make the action of the British
Legislature subservient to their class and
personal interests? There is no way open for
the people but to overcome this class arro-
gance in stout combat. Honest elections wemust
have if we are to expect equitable laws. The
future of the nation demands this, and should
have it even though the House of Lords went
finally down in the struggle. The nation can
live without such a Houss, and if it becomes
troublesomely obstructive, there will not be
much hesitation in setting about its abolition.
Picturesque and ornamental it may be; but
sound, honest, and wise lawmaking is more
essential; and if our people have to ask them-
selves whether they prefer an honest repre-
sentation in the Commons, or a number of
ornamental persons in an Upper House, they
will most assuredly sacrifice questionable
ornament to that which may be regarded as
essential for healthy national life.

J.P., was proved at Wakefield, on the 27th ult.,
under £BOO,OOO personalty, by the executors, John
Crossley, his brother; Edward Crossley, Louis
John Crossley, and Henry Crossley, his nephews;
and Bonj4min Musgrave, of Moth Park, Halifax,
to each of whom he leaves a legacy of £4OO. The
will is dated Nov. 7, 1868, with two codicils,
1869-71 ; and the testator died Jan. 5 following,
aged 64. Ho leaves to his son, now Sir Savile
Brinton Crossley, Bart., his estate and mansion at
Somerleyton, and other estates in Suffolk and
Norfolk. Ile leaves to his wife an annuity of
£6,000, his residence Bellevue, all jewels, personal
ornaments, carriages, horses, wines and consum-
able stores, and the use of plate, books, statues,
pictures, and furniture. To each of his daughters
a legacy of £50,000. The residue of his property
to be divided into as many shares (and one over)
as there are sons living, the elder taking one share
more than the others. He leaves to his coachman,
butler, footman, wife's lady's-maid, and to
three workmen, £lOO each (free). Ho bequeaths
to the London Missionary Society, West
Riding Yorkshire Home Missionary Society,

Airedale College, each £1,000; to the Congrega-

trustees to perform and fulfil the covenants con-
tained in the deed (1868) for founding the Crossley
Orphan Home and School, and devises to his wife
all that piece of land in Skircoat Moor on which
the earns is erected. He leaves directions that
his executors may allow to remain in the company
of John Crossley and Sons (Limited), carpet manu-
facturers, any shares, bonds, and funded stock of
foreign nations connected therewith. The testator

of upwards of 8,000 of the townsmen and towns-

JOSEPH MAZZINI ON THE SOCIAL
QUESTION.

The best answer, says the Emancipazione, which
can be given to the accusation brought against
Joseph Mazzini of want of interest in the economical
welfare of the working classes, is the reproduction
of his works. The following is an article written
upon the social question in 1862, by which work-
ing men may judge how much truth there is in
the imputation :
Many, too many, among you, wrote Mazzini,
are poor. To three-fourths of the men belonging
to the working classes, agricultural or manufactur-
ing, life is a daily struggle to acquire the indis-
pensable means of existence; They work with
their arms, ten, twelve, sometimes fourteen hours
a day, and scarcely obtain the necessaries of
physical life by this assiduous, monotonous, and
irksome labour. To teach these the duty of
making progress, to speak to them of intellectual
and moral life, of political rights, of education, is
mere irony during the present social order. They
have neither time nor means of making progress.
Enfeebldd, weary, almost stupefied by a life spent
within the narrow circle of a few mechanical opera-
tions, they learn a mute, impotent, often unjust, ran-
cour against the class to which their employers
belong ; they seek oblivion of their present trouble,
and of the uncertainity of the future in the stimulus
of strong drink, and sleep in places more worthy the
name of dens than of rooms, to wake again to the
same exertion of physical strength. This con-
dition is sad in the extreme, and must be changed.
You are men, and as such have faculties not
physical only, but intellectual and moral, which
it is your duty to develop° ; you must be citizens
and as such, should, for the good of all, exercise
rights which require a certain degree of education
and a certain amount of time. It is clear that you
should work less and earn more than you now
do. Being all sons of God, and his brothers, we
are called to form one great fsmily. Inequalities
may arise in this family, generated by different
aptitudes, capacities, and differing love of work ;
but one principle must rule them, " whoever is
disposed to give as much work as he is able, for
the common weal, should obtain sufficient re-
muneration to render him capable of developing
his own life more or less, under all the aspects
which go to complete it." This is the ideal to
which we should study the means of approaching
from century to century. Every change, every
revolution which does not draw a step nearer to it,
which does not make social progress correspond
with political progress, which does not in a
measure promote the improvement of the poorest
classes, violates the divine plan, resolves itself into
a war of faction against faction in search of illigiti-
mate dominion, and is an evil and a lie. But how
far can we now proceed towards this end ? And
how and by what means can we attain it ?
Some among your more timid friends have sought
the remedy in the morality of the working-man,
while establishing savings-banks and other similar
institutions. They have said to the working man,
bring your wages here, economize, abstain from all
excess in drink or in anything else; emancipate
yourselves from misery by privation. And
these aro excellent counsels, because they aim
at the moral improvements of the working-
man, without which all reforms are useless. But
they neither solve the question of the misery of
which I speak, nor take social duty into account.
Very few of you can save out of your wages, and
those few can, by slowly hoarding, partly provide
for old ago; but the economical question should
aim at provision for the prime of life, for the
development and possible expansion of life while
it is active, vigorous, and capable of efficiently
ministering to the progress of the fatherland and
of humanity. Besides, society, which lives by
their labour, and whenever threatened claims a
tribute of blood from the sons of the people, owes
them a sacred debt. Others, who are not enemies
to, but careless of, the people and of the cry of
anguish which bursts from the hearts of the men
of toil, fearful of potent innovations, and bound to
a school of so-called economists, who have ,
meritoriously and advantageously fought all the
battles of free-trade, but without turning their
minds to the necessity of progress and association
(in themselves inseparable from human nature),
have maintained and do maintain, like the
philan-
thropists of whom I spoke just now, that everyone
can, even under existing conditions, build up his
own independence by his own activity; that any
change in the constitution of labour would be
superfluous or hurtful; and that their firmula is
sufficient to create by degrees an approximate
equilibrium of comforts among the classes which
constitute society.
Freedom of internal traffic, freedom of trade
between nations, progressive diminution of duties
specially on raw material, general encouragement
given to great manufacturing undertakings, to the

multiplication of means of communication, to
machinery rendering production more active, so
much may, aecording to the economists, be done
by society ; any further intervention on its side is,
according to them, a source of evil. If this were
true, the disease of indigence would be incurable ;
and, God forbid, my brothers, that I should ever
give this despairing, atheistic, and immoral
answer to your complaints and aspirations. God
has devised a better future for you which is not
contained in the remedies of the economists.
These remedies, in fact, only aim at the possible
increase for a certain time of the production of
wealth, not at making a more equal distribution
of it.

While philanthropists contemplate the man
alone, and exert themselves to render him more
moral without undertaking the increase of the
common wealth so as to give him a field for self-
improvement, the economists only look to fertiliz-
ing the sources of production without taking
account of the man. Under the exclusive system of
freedom which they preach, and which has, more
or less, regulated the economical world in our own
times, the existence is proved by undeniable docu-
ments of an increase in productive activity and in
capital, not of universally diffused prosperity;
the misery of the working classes is the same as
before.

Freedom of competition is a delusion for him
who, not being able to save out of his daily
wages, has nothing wherewith to initiate;
competition is a delusion, just as political
liberty is a delusion to him who, wanting
education, instruction, means and time, , can-
not exercise his rights. The increase of
facilities of traffic, the progress of means of
communication will by degrees emancipate labour
from the tyranny of tradesmen, of the interme-
diate class between production and consumers;
but they will not avail to emancipate him from the
tyranny of capital, they will nut give the means
of labour to him who has them not. For want of
an equal distribution of wealth, of a more just
apportionment of products, of a progressive increase
in the number of consumers, capital itself is with-
drawn from its true economical end, and becomes
partly stagnant in a few hands. Instead of being all
distributed in the circulation, it is directed towards
the production of superfluous objects, of luxury, of
fictitious needs. Instead of being concentrated on
ho production of the objects of the first necessity
to life, it is risked in perilous and often immoral
speculations. Capital is now—and this is the
disease of the present social economy—the despot
of labour.

Of the three classes which now make up
society economically—capialists, that is, pos-
sessors of the means or instruments of labour,
lands, factories, raw materials; contractors, em-
ployers of labour, tradesmen who represent or
ought to represent the intellect ; and operatives,
I who represent manual labour. The first alone is
I master of the position, and has the power of pro-
moting, retarding, accelerating and directing
labour towards certain ends. Its part in the
necessaries of labour, in the value of production is
comparatively determined; the place of the instru-
ments of labour does not vary save within known
and restricted limit; and time, up to a oertain
point at least, is its own, not in the powerof absolute
need. The part of the second is uncertain,
dependent on their intellect, on their activity,
but especially on circumstances; on the greater or
lesser development of competition and on the ebb
and flow of capital in consequence of events which
cannot be calculated upon. The part of the last,
of the operatives, consists in wages determined
before the work, and without regard to the greater
or lesser utility of the enterprise, and the limits
within which wages range are determined by the
relation existing between labour offered and
labour asked for; in other words, between the
population of operatives and capital.
Now the first, tending to increase, and to an
increase which generally exceeds the second, even
though by a little, wages tend to fall, where other
causes do not intervene. And time is not in the
hands of the working man—the financial and poli-
tical crisis, the sudden application of machinery to
the different branches of manufacturing industry,
the irregularity of production, and its tendency
to accumulate in one direction only, an insepar-
able result of unenlightened competition, the
unequal distribution of the working population
on certain points or on certain branches of activity,
and ten other causes interrupting labour do not
leave the operative a free choice of his conditions.
,On one side of him stands absolute misery, on the
other the acceptance of any compact which may
be offered.

Such a state of things has within it, I
repeat, the germs of a sore which must be
cured. The remedies proposed by the economists
are inefacient for the purpose. There is, never*

theless, progress in the class to which you belong,
an historical, continuous progress, which has
overcome many another. diffieulty. You were
slaves, you were serfs, you are now p tid workmen.
You emancipated yourselves from slavery, from
serfdom; why should you not emancipate your-
selves from the yoke of wages to become free
producers, masters of the whole value of the
production which results from you labour? Why,
be ween your work and the work of society which
has sacred duties towards its members, should not
the greatest, the finest revolution imaginable be
Peacefully accomplished, that which, giving labour
as the economical basis of human association, and
the fruits of labour as the basis of property, shall
under one single law of equilibrium between pro.
duction and consumption, without distinction of
class, without the tyrannical predominance of one
of the elements of labour over the other, collect
all the sons of the same mother country?

The first of a series of conferences of Mom.
hers of Parliament, working-men, and others,
took place at the Century Club, Pall Mall, on
Friday evening last, under the auspices of the
Labour Representation League.
Mr. Walter Morrison, M.P., presided, and
Mr. Thomas Hare, barrister, read a paper on
the above-named subject, in which he advo-
cated that charitable bequests, particularly
when consisting of landed property, should ho
administered by the State, by means of
popularly elected overseers, as was proposed
by Sir C. Dillte and others in the Lands and
Commons, Preservation Bill, now before Par-
liament, in place of being controlled, as they
at present were, by governors, trustees, or
vestries. He thought, by such a plan, ths
principle of co-operation in the cultivation
of the soil might be advantageously ap-
plied. Ho was opposed to the views of
Sir C. Trevelyan, for converting, by sale or
other form, these public benefactions into
private property. Ho suggested that the
eleemosynary charities, which in London
alone amounted to £BO,OOO per annum, should
be at once reformed in their administration,
so that their action should not affect, as it now
does, the pauperization in spirit of the reci-
pients; and that educational endowments,
estimated in the metropolis at £llO,OOO per
annum, should be so re-modelled in their con-
ditions as to secure to the labouring classes,
through their offspring, for whose benefit the
estates were originally devised, a good tech.
nical—and especially when talent was evinced
—a higher eaucation. In proof of mis-man-
agement he adduced the case of St. Botulph's,
Aldgate, Hackney Estate, now realizing
£7,000 per annum, and yet only educating 100
children at Aldgate parish, to the total neglect
of the dense population at Hackney and White-
chapel, where the income of the charity was
created and raised. The Bill of Sir C. Dilke
was again alluded to by Mr. Hare, as a step
in the right direction for removing some part
of these inequalities.
The discussion was continued by Messrs.
Campin, Mottershead, Brighty, Boon,
Rytin, the Chairman, and Mr. Lucraft, who
expressed himself strongly against a Bill now
before Parliament which proposed to deal
with the Emanuel Hospital Endowments,
which he averred were left for the sole benefit
of the indigent of Westminster, but it was
now sought, through legislation, to misappro-
priate £l,ooo for building a middle-class
boarding school twenty miles from Loudon,
while other sums were to be filched from the
same source to support it when built. He
denounced the sehetne as a barefaced robbery
of the neglected poor.
The Conference closed with thanks to th•
Chairman and Mr. Hare.

REVIEWS,

Royal and Republican France. Two vols. By
HENRY REEVE, Corresponding Member of
the French Institute. (London: Longmans,
Green and Co.)
In 1835, Mr. Reeve, in his preface to his
translation of Tocqueville's " Democracy in
America," treated the public to certain well
composed sentences on contending principles
in government, which, though not very .pro-
found, were appropriate enough, as the indi-
vidual opinions of a man who had made a
very good translation of an interesting and
able work.
The essays now published will not greatly
improve Mr. Reeve's reputation as a political
thinker. They read well and are interesting
enough; but they scarcely ever touch the
root of the matter, and throw no new light
either on the past history or future pro-
spects of France. Read as they appeared in
the " Edinburgh," "Quarterly," and "British
and Foreign Reviews," they. would satisfy
those whose minds were previously prepared
by a perusal of the leaders in our daily news-
papers, anti whose convictions could not he
much disturbed by the facts and reasoning of
Mr. Reeve. Nobody can object to his estimate
of Marie Antoinette; such a woman by her
unhappy fate at least demands our pity; and
as for the rest, opinions will vary to the end of
the world. That the first French revolution
called out some of the vilest as well as some of
thenoblest traits in its prominent actors is what
every reader is by this time aware of. And
that a beautiful woman, who was also a Queen,
suffered through the needless brutality of
certain of her persecutors, is a fact which poli-
tioal writers will not allow to lie by unused.
Just now we are net greatly interested
in the matter except as historical
speculation, especially as Mr. Reeve has
treated us to his thoughts on the more
recent history of France in a way which satis-
fies us that, whatever other quality he may
possess, impartiality is not conspicuous, nor
consistency of thought as complete as it might
be. The following statement of opinion is cer-
tainly confused :
" Whatever may be the opinions we entertain of
the political institutions of the Second Empire, on
the ground of material improvements, it is absurd
to deny that the Emperor rendered great services
to France—services indeed so great that one of the
charges brought against him by his uncorupromis-
ing opponents is, that these benefits caused the
nation to forget even that loss of freedom by which
they have been purchased. However this may be,
nothing is more certain than that the policy which
enriched the rural districts and rebuilt the towns
of France—which is doubling her agricultural pro-
duce, and has more than doubled her foreign trade
—was irreconcilably opposed to the policy of
aggression and war."
Now, the " benefits " conferred by rulers
should he national benefits. We have not to
judge of wise government by the development
of any single interest; noreven by the develop-
ment of all interests unless they are healthily
and permanently developed. Louis Napoleon's
rule in France went on till it broke down ; and
when it did collapse, the ruin was so complete,
the moral as well as material loss to the nation
so stupendous, that to speak of the rule of such
a man as in any way beneficial is simply to
impose on the understanding by words without
plain and honest meaning. The following
passage is slightly contradictory:—
•' Under the reign of the Emperor Napoleon
111., that portion of the Imperial policy which
regarded the rural population was pacific, pro-
gressive, and in some respects liberal; but it was
diametrically opposed to the policy represented by
the great towns and by the spirit of the Revolu-
tion, which tended to Communism, insurrection,
and war. The conflict between these two elements
of his system of government proved fatal to its
permanence. The rural population were sacrificed
to the towns the conservative to the revolutionary
party; the interests of peace to the desperate
chanced of war. We have seen the result, for the
French nation had in reality given pledges to peace
greater than they were perhaps themselves aware
of; and t.tl the true interests of the country have
buffeted from hostilities with a powerful enemy, in
" trout propmtion to the prosperity they had
prevnlv httain ed , end the yet more brilliant
promises of the future."
If the Imperial policy was pacific and pro-
gressive for the rural population, how could
that population be at the same time sacrificed
to the towns? Or how can the writer speak
of the rule of such a man as pacific) in any
sense, except in hould professions. To say
nothing of China and other eastern fightings,
Was there not an Italian war, a Crimean war,
a Mexican war, and finally a German war?
But it would be a waste of time to attempt
any condemnation of such a man. He has
fallen covered with infamy, and the verdict
pronounced by the almost universal conscience
is not likely to be at any time reversed.
It would be wrong not to say that, notwith-
standing the drawbacks pointed out, there is
much interesting reading in Mr. Reeve's
volumes, and, although sometimes inaccurate,
they are at least not dull, and there is the addi-
tional satisfaction to be gained in their peru.-
sal by a consciousness that the writer is
thoroughly sincere, and believes very honestly
La all he has to say.

Midnight Webs. By G. M. FENN. (Tinsley

Biothers).
We wonder if it is possible to find out what
stories may be regarded as good stories for
boys. The publishers and authors ought to
have settled this question long ago. But boys,
like men, may have their fashions, and the
seven champions of Christendom, and Robin-
sin Crusoe perhaps are as unfitted for their
tastes to-day, as Toni Jones and Roderick
Random for the tastes of their fathers. Of
course, it does not do under any circumstances
to bore young readers with prosy reflections,
however wholesome in themselves; and as for
morals, whether placed at the foot of the story
to be skipped, or run through it, to sicken
the juvenile reader, they never were relished
by boys, and what is more they never will be.
But in giving notion and incident, should
not a sound discretion be used so as to
keep clear of that plethora of blood and
violence which harden the feelings and
too frequently deprave the heart? " Under
the Tree Ferns" is a story of New Zealand,
with more than enough of objectionable
human butcher-work in it. The tale of the
Indian mutiny is very horrible, but very likely
falls short of the truth, as adult readers can
easily understand. But is it necessary boys
should be fed on such incidents as pabulum for
mental growth, or even as temporary excite-
ment? Mr. Fenn can do better, and his effort
should be to do his best. What we say here
is not a charge against him specially. He
offends in this respect with a large number of
writers, and we point this out because we be-
lieve he can rise above it, which is what can-
not be truly said of many of those in whose
company he sins.

BALLOT BILL.

On the Order of the Day for going into
Committee on the Parliamentary and Munici-
pal Elections Bill, in the Lords, on Monday,
- Lord Cairns pointed out that the clauses had
been reduced by one-half as compared with
the Bill of last year, in order that provisions
should be taken out of the Bill and put into
the schedule. He protested against a system
which was liable to great abuse.
The House having gone into Committee,
Lord Colchester moved to omit clause 1, abolish-
ing the present system of election nomination.
Lord Ripon defended the clause as conducive
to the quiet and orderly character of elections,
and the clause was retained. _ _ _

On Clause 2, enacting that the votes shall be
taken by Ballot,
The Duke of Richmond said that the clause
opened up the whole question of personation
—an offence so serious that it was absolutely
necessary to provide some machinery by which
the vote could be traced. In the Bill of 1870,
which had upon its back the name of Mr.
Bright, Lord Hartington proposed a clause to
this effect, which he had taken out, and now
proposed for adoption.
Lord Ripon pointed out various points of
difference between the present Bill and that of
Lord Hartington. The amendment was really
vital to the Bill, because it would render secret
voting almost impossible.
Lord Cairns contended that the clause would
be productive of mischief, vice, perjury, and
fraud, and that unless personation were to be
triumphant it must be followed and punished
by means of a scrutiny.
The Lord Chancellor said that the amend-
ments of the Duke of Richmond would, if
adopted, make this an entirely new Bill. It
was not worth while, for the sake of punish-
ing the small medium of personation, to lose
the larger benefit of an absolutely secret
vote.
Lord Grey was afraid that personation was
already no infiniteLimal evil, and that under
the Ballot it might be carried on to a much
greater extent.
Lord Itomilly held that the only effectual
method of putting down personation was by a
greater multiplication Atha number of polling
plo ces.
The Duke of Somerset said that the object
of the Ballot was to obtain an honest vote and
asked whether the Government intended to
adopt the words they regarded as so desirable
in: 1870.
'Lord Granville said it was oarrying the
argumentunt ail hontznem too far to hold the
Government responsible for not adopting a
clause which, indeed, had not been fully
argued two years ago.
Their Lordships divided, when the Duke of
Richmond's amendment was carried by a
majority of 71, the Contents being 162 and the
Not-Contents 91.
The Duke of Richmond next proposed an
amendment raising the question of secrecy and
making the Ballot optional.
Lord Ripon said it would have been better
to throw out the Bill on the second reading
than to adopt amendments which would render
it a delusion and a sham.
Lord Salisbury denied that the sense either
of the country or the House of Commons
could be pleaded in favour of a compulsory
Ballot.
Lord Cowper opposed the amendment.
Lord Grey could not support an amendment
which was inconsistent with the principle of
the Bill, and virtually destructive of the mea-
sure.
Lord Lyttleton had voted against the Bill
on the second reading, but would be no party
to an amendment that would make the Bill an
utter unreality.
Lord Airlie, who had voted with the Duke
of Richmond in the last division thought that
their Lordships would place themselves in a
false position by agreeing to this amend-
ment.

Lord Cairns denied that the Opposition were
now attempting to defeat the Bill by a side
wind. The Duke of Richmond had given full
notice of the amendments he intended to pro-
pose in Committee, and the Legislature had no
right to impose secrecy upon an eleotor against
his will.
Lord Kimberley contended that if the Bill
passed with these amendments it would be so
much waste paper.
Lord Romilly, having gone through five or
six severely-contested elections, testified to
the strong desire for the Ballot among the
constituencies as a protection against intimida-
tion.
Their Lordships divided, when there ap.
peared a majority of 16 for the Duke of Rich-
mond's amendments Contents, 83; Not-
The Duke of Richmond: not proposed to
strike out certain words in clause 4 prohibiting
Returning Officers, &a., from communicating
how any person votes. Now that the Ballot
W5B optional, no purpose could be served by
this proviso. The amendment was resisted by
Lord Ripon, but was carried on a division by
a majority of 16.
The Duke of Richmond next moved an
amendment to clause C), giving every elootor

so far as is reasonably practicable, a polling-
place within two miles of his residence, instead
of four as proposed by the Bill. The amend-
ment was opposed by the Government, but
was carried on a division by a majority of
19.

On the motion of the Archbishop of Canter-
bury, Clause (3 was amended by striking out
the words permitting Returning Officers to
take any Parliamentary-aided school for the
purposes of the poll.
Lord Shaftesbury proposed two amend-
ments, which he said had found great favour
with the elite of the working men, and which
together would be eminently favourable to the
peace and good order of elections. The first,
enabling the poll at borough elections to be
prolonged until 8 o'clock p.m. The second,
closing all the public-houses on the polling
-
day. The first was carried by 97 against 72
votes.

Lord Cairns moved that the Chairman re-
port progress, in order to call attention to
conduct on the part of the Government which
was entirely unprecedented within his ex-
perience. Having by their organ, Lord Ripon,
refused to accede to the amendment, they
suddenly turned round, and all of them
went into the lobby with Lord Shaftesbury,
This was speaking one way and voting
another.

Lord Ripon said he had regretted that the
other House had struck out the clause lengthen-
ing the hours of the polling, but thought the
hour of 8 in the evening too late throughout
the year. He had voted for the clsuse with
the view of modifying it on the report.
A lively and somewhat acrimonious die-.
oussion now sprang up, in which "words ot
heat," were exchanged between the leading
occupants of the benches on both sides. Lord
Salisbury extenuated the conduct of the Go-
vernment on the ground that, having had an
"unfortunate evening," they saw an oppor•
tunity of being in a majority for once. Lord Bath
made a personal attack on the Lord Chancellor.
Lord Granville warmly defended tlxe Lord
Chancellor, and said that noble Lords opposite
were so accustomed to exercise a despotism
over the House that they could not conceive
any course for the Government except to be
beaten. The imputation of " despotism " was
resented by the Duke of Richmond as a personal
reflection, and, as such, was indignantly re-
pudiated. Lord Clanricarde called upon the
Clerk to read the Standing Order against
"sharp and taxing speeches."
Ultimately the motion for reporting progres
was withdrawn, and Lord Kimberley having
announced that the Government would cer-
tainly go into the lobby against Lord Shaftes-
bury's second amendment, it was rejected by
133 votes against 90. The result of the two
divisions is that the poll will be kept open
until eight o'clock p.m., while the public-
houses will be allowed to remain open during
the day of election as usual.
Lord. Beauchamp moved to add words to
clause 33, limiting the operation of the Act to
December 31, 1880, unless Parliament should
otherwise determine. The amendment was
strongly opposed by the Government, but it
was carried on a division by 106 votes
against 69.
The Duke of Richmond's form of Ballot
paper was also carried against that in the Bill
by 91 votes against 59.
.The Bill was then ordered to be reported
with amendments.

to 1.

articles.text:
THE POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH

SERVIOE.

Amongst our friends and acquaintances, to
the coming of none do we look more hopefully
than to the expected visit of our letter-carriers
Even at times when we momentarily dread
the delivery, by our local and adhesive friend,
of a missive fraught with news the most
frigorio, cheerless, hopeless, and bad, the
sound of his foot-tread on our doorstep, and
the "What news ?" performed by him on our
knocker, east over our senses a hopeful ray.
As a rule, our adhesive friends look blithe and
merry, are light of foot, and of pleasing man-
ners. A few "surly hounds" may be found
amongst them, but they are the universally
acknowledged ours of the pack, and are not of
it. Yet our adhesive friends have little (muse
for heartiness of soul in the brilliant prospects
the arduous occupations they follow offer to
them, either present or prospective. Their
wage is small, progresses with a snail-like
pace, and culminates in slipshod, and a small
pension should life be spared to a useless state
of bodily powers for other employment, and
no cause arise to call for prior dismissal.
The hours in which they are daily engaged in
connection with their calling are viciously too
long, bearing in mind its perambulatory, its
Zigzag, and up-and-down-doorstep character.
Ten or twelve hours daily devoted to the pub-
lic service by our letter-carriers, crippling the
agile, putting old heads on young shoulders,
and consigning those of mature and middle
ages very frequently to premature graves.
These things the. public, and we of it, do not
hold with; and most earnestly do we ask of
the present progressive, highly-intellectual,
and common-sense postal Board, on behalf of
our adhesive friends, increase of pay, increase
of numbers, increase of opportunity for ad-
vancement, and decrease in the number of
hours for labour. Heart and lung diseases,
rheumatism, and premature decay from many
causes are not the exception amongst our
letter-carriers, and few medical practitioners
in London and its environs but know this fact
right well, fur better than the Post Office
Medical authorities, for obvious reasons. We
submit a simple remedy—and a cheap one,
after all—to lessen these evils, and to stamp
out that growing one, DISCONTENT.—The
Medical Press and Circular.

SERVANTS' AID SOCIETY.

A crowded meeting of domestic servants was
held on Tuesday at 48, Great Marlborough-street,
under the presidency of. the Marquis Townshend.
The Chairman said the meeting had been called
to promote a society, having for its object the
improvement of the social position of the domestic
servant. He considered the time had arrived when
domestic servants should take care of their own
interests, and there was no institution in existence
which properly represented the interests .of the
class which this society was intended to benefit.
The society had begun in an humble way, but had
made very satisfactory progress in enrolling mem-
bers. lie believed the interests of masters and
servants were one, and he hoped the society would
receive the support of masters and mistresses.
About 100 members had joined the society, and it
had a respectable balance in hand. Amongst the
objects of the society were the assistance of ser•
vants in sickness and while out of employment, and
to relieve distress in old age by pensions.
The meeting was addressed by the Rev. Mr.
Thomas, Rev. Mr. Gibson, Mr. Passey, and others
in support of the society, and a resolution passed
pledging the support of those present. Upwards
of 80 persons enrolled their names.

The vote of thanks to the chairman concluded
the proceedings.

CONVICT LABOUR.

On Tuesday night a public meeting was called
in the Boys' School-room, Theobald's-road, Hol-
born, to hear a statement of the condition to which
mat-makers have been reduced by the competition
of prison labour. Mr. W. T. IsPOullagh Torrens,
M.P., presided. The subject did not appear to
excite much public interest. The Chairman said
he considered that honest men, living by labour
outside the walls of a prison, ought to be the first
care of the law, and not the rogue inside. If
prison labour was allowed to interfere with the
free sale and marketable value of that of the honest
man, it was a discouragement of free industry,
and could never servo the true interests of society
The true kind of prison labour was that which
taught a caged man that he was not to be supported
altogether at the public expense, but that he was
to:work fur his own bread; and the ingenuity of
the law, Mr. Torrens contended, ought to be

applied to find out those means of accomplishing
that end which did not perceptibly interfere with
free labour. He advised a petition to be sent to
both Houses of Parliament on the subject.
Colonel Beresford, M.P., moved a resolution
recognising the soundness of the principle of
remunerative convict industry, but asserting that
the employment of convicts in mat making—a
market already overstocked—was opposed to every
doctrine of commercial economy, that it led to the
impoverishment and pauperisation of honest labour,
and that applied to other pursuits, convict labour
was much more productive and less objectionable.
The gallant colonel expressed a strong sympathy
for the class in whose interest the meeting was
held, and he said no more just cause than theirs
had ever been submitted to the Houses of Parlia-
ment. He adduced particulars to prove this, and
concluded by expressing his faith that a change of
Government would bring about redress.

Mr. Adams seconded the resolution, and said he,
as one of the class affected, many of whom did
not earn more than 12s. a week, craved for inquiry
into the truth of his statement. The resolution
was carried, as was also a second resolution, direct-
ing an appeal to the Legislature at the earliest
possible opportunity "for fair play." A vote of
thanks to the chairman closed the proceedings.

instructed to draw your attention to the Ist and
2nd explanatory sub-sections of the Ist section of
the Act beginning with "being a master," which
clauses are professedly inserted for the protection
of the workmen. At present the Act is administered
by employers of labour, but a bench of magis-
trates consisting of working men might, with
perfect fairness, construe these clauses so as to
prevent an employer from dismissing or refusing
to employ a workman for any cause whatsoever.
Although this may appear an absurd construction,
yet, if you will consider the decisions which have
been given by magistrates, who are themselves
employers, we feel sure you will admit that they
have been equally absurd, and a law which is
susceptible of, such abuse we respectfully submit
ought not to remain on the statute book. Also the

employers and workmen, and quite without the
province of tke:criminal law; therefore, we hope
and trust that you will see these objections to the
proposed Bill in the same light as we do, and pro-
pose these Omissions at the same time. I am
requested to remind you that, although we submit
these amendments for your consideration, we are
still of opinion the Bill ought to be repealed.

up its project of sending a deputation to M.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SlR,—Being a thoroughgoing trades unionist
myself, and as I believe
,you to be the same,
1 beg to be allowed a short space in the next
issue of your valuable paper in the hope that
either you, or some one of your numerous corre-
spondents, will answer the following questions,
—viz., does the real strength of trades
unionism consist in the officers, of one trades
council going to another town (during the
excitement of a pending .election) to speak in
opposition'to what they themselves believe to
be the Wish of the trades council of the town
they visit, and what mast be the consequences of
such a proceeding? I have . been led to ask
these questions because I, understand the
president and secretary of the Manchester and
Salf,md Trades Council made it their bilsiness
to come to Oldham .a day or two before the
late election to speak in favour of the Tory
candidate, and in opposition to the Oldham
Trades Council, who,they pretended, had taken
some action in favour of the Liberal, candi-
date. Now; Sir, another question arises here; ,
would not the Oldham Trades Council have
been perfectly justified if they had have taken'
such a step, if they really were of the opinion
that it would be for the advantage of the
various trades societies in their town for
them to do so and if this is so, I should like
to ask by what right did the officers of the
Manchester and Salford Trades Council come
to Oldham to act in opposition and if possible
Make their efforts .of more effect, and as a
natural consequence spread discord, division,
and enmity in their ranks? Is this the
'unity" that !` i strength" that Mr. Wood is
so very fond of talking about. I find that Mr.
Wood's speech was considered of so much
importance by the
.Tory party (and in pro-
portion telling against the Oldham Trades
Council) that the Oldham, Standard Specially
referred to it in a leader. For my own part
can see nothing in it but the old out and dried
blate against the present Government, which
any honest and intelligent person would
be ashamed of. He did' tell them, that he did
not know anything about this Stanley,although
this Stanley was chosen by the factory opera-
tives of Oldham to be their arbitrator in the
dispute with their employers, and he pretends
to be a great friend of theirs, and will do
almost anything to assist them to shorten the
hours of labour. He did tell them, also, that
ho knew a great
,deal about the nondescript
Radical-Tory, Mr. Cobbett. He also spoke
about the Criminal Law Amendment Act, but
only to be condemned as an Act of the present
Government; he had, not the manliness to say
a single word against those Members (whom
he supports), that passed it into law against
that Uovernment ; oh, no, of course not ; no
doubt he thinks they ought to. be considered
but very little less than angels for doing it.
, Would it be it all surprising, if the present
Government was to ,go out of office, and the
Tory party come into power, if' this con-
sistent trades unionist were to turn round and
tell his friends (the Tory working men) that
this obnoxious law was now become the most
beautiful and beneficial measure imaginable,
and would continue to be so as long as their
party. were in office? It could not by chance do
them any harm ; they (the Tories) would take
care of that; but remember, that if the
Liberals corns+ again into power you must work
with might and main; and net rest until it is
totally repealed. I take the 'liberty to add,
that i think this would be quite consistent for
any person to do, who, after voting in his own
town for the very men that helped to make this
abominable Act what it is, then goes to another
town to assist to send another member of the
same stamp to the House of Commons, to make
the galling yoke heavier. Such trades union-
ists may do for the refined city of Manchester,
but they will,not do for the rough yeas" of
" Ovvdhani," ; they cannot swallow it.—l am,
yours respectfully,
A MEMBER OF THE TRADES COUNCIL.
. Oldham, June 17.

THE CURRENCY.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sut,—Aa you have opened your columns to
a discussion of the currency question, I venture
to say a few words on that very enticing sub-
ject. Ti the theory of the currency nothing
new can be added; never was a subject worked
so threadbare.

The practice is, however, bad, and. arises, I
fancy, from a confusion of ideas. No doubt
the circulation ought to be based on a precious
metal, but it does not necessarily follow that
that metal should be coined—it is no more the
duty of Government to give change for a five
-
pound note than for a sovereign.
Au issue of inconvertible notes, stopping
whenever the price of gold reached 44 Per
ounce, would meet Sir ltobert Peel'* theory,
and according to experience gained by the

working of the present law, 40 millions would
naturally circulate, giving a saving at 3 per
cent. of £1,200,000 per annum.—l am, Sir,
your obedient servant,

W. FIELD.

THE POSTMAN'S GRIEYANCES
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE,

Sia,—ln walking through the arch in John
William-street, about 5.40 a.m. on Monday
morning, I was attracted by seeing the Post-
master of Huddersfield apparently reading one
of ' the
,plaoards headed "Letter Carriers'
Appeal.' After watching him for a moment,
I saw him take a penknife and deliberately
cut the placard twice across each way, and
after that pall it into shreds. I called out to
him and charged him with the act he had
committed,

Sir, I think a gentleman in his position,
however he may differ from Alio men, ought in
common justice to let their property alone.
I will now leave the public to judge, and con-
clude, yours respectfully,
FArn PLAY.
Huddersfield, June, 1872.

articles.text:
CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT,

1871, AMENDMENT BILL.
To the Editor of the BEE-HEVE,

Sin,—Would you kindly allow me a short
space,in your very, valuable pdper, to say that,
at a meeting of the Nottingham Trades Union
Association, held at the Talbot Inn, Long-
row, June 6, I was directed to write to your
paper to the ilea that I was. much as the
Association was formed, to watch the working
of the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1871,
with a view to its total repeal. They feel
called upon to take some action respecting the
Bill introduced to the House of Commons by
Mr. Vernon Harcourt and Others. WhiJer
according to the Parliamentary Committee of
the Trades Union Congress honest and good
intentions we feel full assured the adopting
of their Bill will have the very opposite effect
to what they intended. In no way ean their
Bill be said to simplify the ambiguities of the
present law; the legal course would still be
as uncertain. Neither do we think there has
been a single conviction under the present law
which would have been obviated by the pro-
posed one. Nay, by it confusion is worse con-
founded, The introduction of a now feature
of the most subtle and illusory nature, viz.,
the motive will, I think, be attended by the
moot direful consequences. Suppose a man,
before the unpaid magistracy, charged with
"standing, speaking-, looking," or it might be,
"whistling, laughing, or crying," with a
view to intimidate or coerce. How is he to
prove the motive which actuated him into
doing? and we feel sure this could and will be
done under the proposed Bill. Take this case
—a man took an honourable and prominent
part in the affairs of the Nine Hours League
in this town. Certain employers have said,
in consequence of this, they would give £lOO
to any man who could invent or prove a
charge against him to criminate him, and the
week before last they really thought they were
successful. They induced a man to apply for
a summons against him, and employed a soli-
citor to advise him, for calling hun a black
sheep. The summons was granted readily,
but afterwards withdrawn. His non-society
pals resisted all offers, and resolved to give
true evidence. No more was heard of it. The
fact of the matter was, in conversation with
the foreman of the shop, he said—" I took a
walk by the Trent side yesterday, and I saw a
man leaning against a gate crying. I asked
what ailed him, and he said these five sheep
have strayed from you field, and are so foot-
sore, I fear I shall not be able to get them
back again." I maintain there was nothing
criminal in these words, but under the pro-
posed Bill I fear they could have successfully
argued criminal intent; for these reasons we
urge the withdrawal of the Bill, or that all
friends of trade unions—and they are not few,
and not without
__influence—to petition for its
rejection.
I am further directed to write to Mr. Herbert
and Seely, and also the Secretary of the
Trades' Union Parliamentary Committee, to
this effect, Hoping you will be able to find
space for this,-1 remain, yours respectfully,
ALFRED THORNTON, Secretary.
49, Trueman-street, Alfred-street, Central.

Accounts from the provinces testify to the
destructive nature of the recent thunder-
storms. The Manchester express which left
St. Pancras Station at five o'clock on Tuesday
afternoon, ran into some debris which had
been washed by the heavy rain upon the line
close to the mouth of the Peak Forest Tunnel,
near Chapel-en-le-Frith, and some of the pas-
sengers were injured.
Mr. S. C. Whitbread having declined, on
account of his advanced years, to come for-
ward as a Liberal candidate for Bedfordshire,
Mr. Francis Basset, banker, of The Heath,
Leighton Buzzard, has consented to stand
conditionally on the Marquis of Tavietock
being brought out to contest the county when
he attains his majority. The Marquis is the
eldest son of the now Duke of Bedford, and is
20 years of age,

The American Government has ordered that
the British subject recently abducted from
Canada should be returned, and indemnified
for his false arrest.

In the railway accident which happened
lately. at Juisvy, on the Orleans line, the
Marquise Paniera, the mother of the Duchesse
de Malakoff, was killed.

The Spanish Minister of Finance has sent
instructions to London for the payment of the
coupon of the External Debt. Similar orders
have been given to the different capitals where
Spanish bonds are held.

Prince Bismarck has granted permission to
the Gallician Jesuits at Schrimm, who were
ordered to quit Prussian territory, to remain in
Prussia several months longer conditionilly on
their abstaining from receiving confession OA
preaching. The concession is accepted as SW
indication that the Government intends ad-!
ministerinr, leniently the law against the
prose' ibeeorder.

The funeral of the Rev. Dr. Norman Itacleod
took place yesterday, near Glasgow, the ser-
vices being conducted in the Cathedral.

The Directors of the Bank of England have
announced a further reduction in the rate of
discount, from 31 to 3 per cent.

Yesterday was the thirty-fifth apniversary
of the Accesion of Queen Victoria to• the
Crown.

_
The Marquis of Lorne is reported to be sof-
tening from low fever.
The German Parliament yesterday passed the
Bill on the William Luxemburg Railway Con-
vention after its third reading.

A conference will be held this afternoon, at
the Westminster Palace Hotel, to consider the
Building Societies' Bill, now before Parliament.
Strong exception is taken by the Building

Government Amendments.
